10141-a-discourse-on-the-life-character-:
William Cullen Bryant, the poet and editor, gave this memorial address before the New-York Historical Society on May 17, 1870. Its subject was Gulian Crommelin Verplanck, a New York lawyer, scholar, and public man who had just died after a long useful life. The Society asked Bryant to print the address at once.

Bryant traces Verplanck's work in law, letters, and civic life, praising steady service over show. He presents a man whose learning and manners helped shape New York's public mind. Readers get a graceful, period portrait of a respected citizen, and of the city he served.
10517-government-and-rebellion-a-sermon-:
Rev. E. E. Adams preached this sermon in the North Broad Street Presbyterian Church on Sunday morning, April 28, 1861, just after the Civil War began. Published by request, it takes Proverbs 17:11 as text: an evil man seeks only rebellion, and a cruel messenger shall be sent against him. Adams treats rebellion as a crime against God and government.

Adams argues that God never pardons a rebel until he repents and submits, and that people need not pronounce forgiveness until an enemy shows sorrow and stops wrongdoing. A child's rebellion against a parent offers his homely parallel. Readers get a firm, wartime sermon on law, repentance, and Union.
10698-the-aeroplane-boys-on-the-wing-or-:
John Luther Langworthy sent Frank and Andy Bird to the tropics in The Aeroplane Boys on the Wing, published in 1912. The Bird boys, already known to readers of the series, chase a clue that leads to a strange "devil-bird," an airship launch, an air chase, and a camp in the tropical jungle. Guards, firebrands, and jaguars add danger on the ground.

Langworthy writes fast, plain adventure for boys, with the aeroplane itself as the hero's tool. The book is an early example of aviation fiction, written when flying was barely a decade old. Young readers get thrills, teamwork, and exotic places, all from the cockpit of a new machine.
11153-no-hero:
E. W. Hornung wrote this 1903 novel, whose narrator insists his story is unheroic, told in the modern manner from the latest possible point. The book opens with a waiter bringing the narrator a fatal letter from Catherine Evers, the first for years from a once constant correspondent. The narrator, a young man about town on two walking-sticks in 1900, studies the unopened envelope, whose handwriting gives no hint of its news.

Chapters follow a plenipotentiary, the theatre of war, first blood, a marked woman, second fiddle, prayers and parables, the lion's mouth, a stern chase, and number three. Bob Evers tells the narrator that his talk of being mere pals with a woman was rot, as he shaves with razor in mid-air. Hornung, creator of Raffles, writes a wry tale of love, honour, and self-knowledge.
11256-social-life-at-rome-in-the-age-of-:
W. Warde Fowler's study of social life at Rome in Cicero's age fills a gap he saw in English scholarship. readers knew Roman politics, but not Roman manners, education, morals, and religion in the last age of the Republic. Drawing on Cicero's nine hundred surviving letters, the richest social archive from classical antiquity, Fowler reconstructs daily life, households, friendships, and public conduct. Marquardt's Privatleben der Römer supports his account.

Fowler planned the book as a companion to a life of ancient Athens, then finished it as a standalone educational work. Its argument is that Cicero's age matters as much as the Empire's, as a critical moment in Graeco-Roman civilization. Classicists still cite it as an accessible introduction to late Republican society.
11448-cicero:
W. Lucas Collins's Cicero, in the Ancient Classics for English Readers series, surveys the Roman orator's life and work in twelve chapters, from early life and education through the impeachment of Verres. the consulship and Catiline, exile and return, relations with Caesar and Antony, character as politician and orator, correspondence, essays on old age and friendship, philosophy, and religion. Collins acknowledges Forsyth's Life of Cicero and Long's scholarly volumes, taking responsibility for translations.

Collins opens by noting ancient means different things for Homer's infant society and for Cicero's late Republic. His volume aims at general readers, not scholars, summarizing a large career compactly. Students meeting Cicero for the first time will find it a clear, Victorian introduction.
12140-roman-farm-management-the-treatise:
Published in 1918, this volume gives English versions of two Roman farm manuals. Cato wrote on agriculture in the second century BCE, and Varro wrote three books on rural affairs a century later. A Virginia farmer made the translations, with notes that link old practice to his own day. Both books address owners who ran farms with hired hands and enslaved labor.

Cato moves from buying land and laying out a farm to the duties of overseer and housekeeper, soil care, crops, vines, olives, livestock, and even curing hams. Varro divides his subject into the farm itself, its equipment and workers, and its animals, with long passages on fences, water, buildings, and breeding. Together they show how Romans judged soil, planned labor, and weighed profit against pleasure in country life.
13481-roman-life-in-the-days-of-cicero:
The Rev. Alfred J. Church writes Roman life in the days of Cicero as scenes, not as a formal biography or a history of the late Republic. Chapters follow a Roman boy, an undergraduate, a magistrate, a great cause, country life, a great conspiracy, Caesar, Pompey, exile, and Cato, Brutus, and Porcia.

Verres the governor, feasting in Syracuse, seizes a captured pirate prize for himself and deals with young and old by practical greed. Caesar swims to a ship with a manuscript held clear of the water and his cloak in his teeth, then orders a tribe massacred without hesitation. Church lets such scenes show Roman law, war, and politics through the eyes of Cicero's age.
13509-grappling-with-the-monster-or-the-:
T. S. Arthur, author of Ten Nights in a Bar-Room, grapples with strong drink in this temperance volume, subtitled the curse and the cure. He admits embarrassment at the mass of material, with every chapter fit to grow into a book of its own. Illustrations trace the steps from youth to manhood, a confirmed drunkard, and old age as a total wreck.

Arthur shows how moderate drinkers slip into excess, as a depraved appetite strives for mastery from the first indulgence and no man who indulges is absolutely safe. Dr. R. P. Harris adds a chapter on tobacco as an incitant to alcohol and an obstacle to reform. The book is a full Victorian case against drink, built from stories, warnings, and cures.
14260-the-great-events-by-famous-histori:
Volume six of The Great Events by Famous Historians gathers episodes from the Middle Ages. It opens with a note on its binding, a copy of a work by Geoffroy Tory for King Francis the First. Tory, a teacher of letters, set up a press in 1518 and printed Greek and Latin books. The volume moves from episode to episode, told by a historian. It aims to let readers meet the past through scenes.

One episode tells how bishops preached the Fourth Crusade against the Greeks as foes of Rome. Clergy urged war as just, drove women from camp, and set men to confession before the assault. Another episode treats the Mise of Lewes, which freed war prisoners and held princes Edward and Henry as hostages. About five thousand men are said to have fallen on each side at Lewes. The book gives war, law, and faith in strokes.
14682-my-friend-prospero:
Henry Harland's 1904 romance My Friend Prospero opens with a coach drawing up before an Italian castle gateway, where Lady Blanchemain considers a formal garden in April weather. John Lane published the novel in London and New York.

Prospero, a miller in the Austrian sense, a bourgeois without coat-armour, courts Annunziata amid terraced gardens, mimosa, and blackcaps, while society warns against a match across rank. Harland writes with light irony about class and love. The novel is a charming comedy of manners, set in an Italy of gardens and old houses.
14903-the-knights-of-the-white-shield-up:
Edward A. Rand's 1886 boys' book, first in the Up-the-Ladder Club series and dedicated to Ken and the other boys, tells how a club is made. A grand march, an offer for Sunday school scholars, a pammerrammer and the nation's birthday follow, with a sick patriot and a nailed door and window.

An entertainment, a cupola, Aunt Stanshy's boarder and a club in splinters lead to a club mended, a knight going to sea, a trap, a fair and a fire. Rand, author of school and camp series, writes club life as moral adventure: boys learning loyalty, leadership and fair play. The white shield stands for a standard the knights try, and sometimes fail, to live up to.
15122-the-little-colonel-s-hero:
Annie Fellows Johnston's 1902 children's novel brings back Lloyd, the Little Colonel of a Kentucky valley home, for her twelfth birthday. The day opens in gloom: her mother lies ill, her father has gone to town, and no one seems to recall the date. Only her pony Tarbaby offers comfort as she rides down a locust-lined avenue.

What looks like neglect soon turns into surprise, and Lloyd learns lessons in patience, pluck, and kindness through the year that follows. Johnston writes in a warm Southern voice, with dialect speech and country detail. Young readers meet a heroine who grows by facing hurt feelings and small trials with grace.
15202-young-folks-treasury-volume-2-of-1:
Edited by Hamilton Wright Mabie, with Edward Everett Hale as associate editor, this second volume of Young Folks' Treasury gathers myths and legendary heroes for children. Advisers include university presidents, a cardinal, and former presidents Roosevelt and Cleveland. An illustration shows Jason hurling his helmet.

Greek heroes, Norse tales, and other world myths appear in retellings suited to young readers, with heroism, cunning, and wonder at the fore. The series aimed to give children a noble stock of stories. Parents and teachers still use the volume as a solid, old-fashioned introduction to myth.
15359-the-negro:
W. E. B. Du Bois published this history in New York in 1915, with maps of Africa and its peoples. It opens by calling Africa at once the most romantic and the most tragic of continents, then traces its ancient kingdoms, its peoples, and its long contact with Europe and Asia. The book was written for general readers, not only for scholars.

Later parts follow the slave trade, the growth of Black life in America, and the struggle for freedom and full citizenship. Du Bois blends geography, history, and argument, pressing the case that Black history begins in Africa, not in slavery. As an early short history by a leading Black scholar, it still reads as both an introduction and a claim: that this past deserves study on its own terms.
15946-the-original-fables-of-la-fontaine:
La Fontaine's original fables, rendered into English prose by Frederick Colin Tilney, with coloured pictures by the author. J. M. Dent and Sons issued the book in London, with E. P. Dutton in New York, as part of Tales for Children from Many Lands, edited by F. C. Tilney. The fables come in plain prose, not verse, for young readers. Pictures by Tilney himself join the text.

The Two Mules, The Hare and the Partridge, and The Gardener and his Landlord open the set. The Man and his Image, The Animals Sick of the Plague, and The Unhappily Married Man follow, with The Rat Retired from the World, The Maiden, and The Wishes. The Dairy-Woman and her Pail of Milk and The Priest and the Corpse close the sample. The book gives La Fontaine's wit in easy English: beasts that teach men.
1642-euthyphro:
Plato's Euthyphro, translated by Benjamin Jowett, opens in the porch of the King Archon, where Socrates awaits his trial for impiety and meets Euthyphro, a diviner prosecuting his own father for murder. Socrates asks Euthyphro what piety itself is, and the diviner's answers unravel under questioning.

Is the pious loved by the gods because it is pious, or pious because loved? The question, still called the Euthyphro dilemma, drives the dialogue to an open end. The work is a brief, perfect introduction to Socratic method, and to philosophy's first questions about gods and goodness.
16440-the-water-supply-of-the-el-paso-an:
J. L. Campbell's engineering paper tackles a dry-country problem: how to water a railway across 128 miles of New Mexico desert between Carrizozo and Santa Rosa. Rain there averaged under ten inches a year, and well water on the line was poor. The road crossed no streams for hundreds of miles in either direction from El Paso.

Campbell sets out the new supply scheme, with wells, quality tests, and figures, followed by discussion from fellow engineers. The paper is technical and full of tables, aimed at civil engineers rather than casual readers. It stands as a clear record of how railways solved water supply in the arid Southwest.
16605-the-ladies-work-book-containing-in:
John Cassell of London put out this how-to book for home needlework, with steps for knitting, crochet, and point lace. It shows how to cast on, purl, join pieces, form rounds, and cast off, then gives plans for mats, covers, tidies, curtains, and small dress items. Drawings walk the reader through each stitch.

The book is a workbench guide, not a tale: each plan states the stitch, the shape, and the finish in plain order. It suits a reader who wants to make useful house goods by hand, from a baby shoe to a bed quilt. Its value today lies in its clear old craft methods and its full range of home projects.
16626-letters-to-helen-impressions-of-an:
Keith Henderson, an artist on the Western Front, writes to Helen from France in this 1917 volume, with his own illustrations. A first letter, June 6, 1916, finds him on the slowest train that ever limped, after seven hours' sleep, with twenty-eight hours still to go. Crucifix Corner, Bailleul, Fricourt Cemetery, trenches, a wounded tank, and Peronne fill the pictures.

Henderson writes as a painter-soldier, noting color, ruin, and odd beauty amid war. His letters are short and vivid, with secrecy about ports and places. The book gives the Great War through an artist's eyes, tender and unsparing at once.
16672-the-last-journals-of-david-livings:
Horace Waller edited David Livingstone's last journals in Central Africa, volume one covering 1866 to 1868. The journals were saved after the explorer's death, with a narrative of his last moments by his servants Chuma and Susi. Chapter one arrives at Zanzibar, meets the sultan, and faces the slave market, tsetse fly, and sepoys' trouble on the road inland.

Waller's introduction recalls the hope that some journals might survive the disaster. The journals give Africa in Livingstone's own daily words: lakes, peoples, and hardships. Readers of exploration will find a moving, first-hand record of the great traveler's final years.
17024-the-last-journals-of-david-livings:
Horace Waller edited this second volume of David Livingstone's last journals, covering 1869 to his death in 1873. It opens with illness, a slow trip to Ujiji, and a puzzling current in Lake Tanganyika, then follows new probes toward the Lualaba and the Manyuema country. Susi and Chuma, his faithful servants, add a closing tale of his last days and sufferings.

The journals mix fever, desertion, Arab traders, and elephant hunts with notes on peoples, rivers, and beasts. Livingstone writes in short, tired entries that still carry wonder. For readers of exploration, this is the raw, moving end of a great African career, told in the explorer's own worn words.
17042-illustration-of-the-method-of-reco:
This Smithsonian Bureau of Ethnology paper, under director J. W. Powell, shows the method of recording Indian languages, drawn from manuscripts of J. O. Dorsey, A. S. Gatschet, and S. R. Riggs. It opens with an Omaha myth, How the Rabbit Caught the Sun in a Trap, obtained from F. LaFleche by Dorsey, printed in a phonetic script with marks for raised, turned, and dotted letters.

The paper teaches field workers how to write Native speech sounds with exact signs, so words can be read true after the speaker is gone. Its symbols, explained in a transcriber's note, cover nasals, stops, and vowels. Linguists and historians of Native America will find a key early methods paper, short, technical, and full of worked examples.
17370-prehistoric-textile-fabrics-of-the:
William H. Holmes's Bureau of Ethnology paper studies prehistoric textile fabrics of the United States as seen in impressions on pottery. Groups run from cord-marked vessels in Pennsylvania and New York to fabrics from Arizona, Kentucky caves, Swiss lake dwellings, and Ohio mounds. Figures show coffee sacking threads, sections, and ancient cloth patterns pressed into clay.

Holmes reads each impression for weave, thread, and method, turning potsherds into textile history. His paper suits archaeologists and craft lovers who want to see lost cloth through clay. Short and richly pictured, it remains a classic early study of how ancient Americans wove, long before any cloth survived.
18113-history-of-the-expedition-to-russi:
General Count Philippe de Ségur wrote this History of the Expedition to Russia, undertaken by Napoleon in 1812, in a second revised edition printed in London in 1825. Ségur dedicates the work to the veterans of the Grand Army, comrades disarmed by the northern ice.

Book one traces the politics of France and Russia since 1807, with Prussia, Turkey, and Sweden in view. Later books follow the march, the battles, and the dread retreat from Moscow. Ségur writes as a soldier who was there, with grief and pride. It is a classic, first-hand history of the 1812 disaster, still read for its vivid, tragic force.
18279-the-composition-of-indian-geograph:
J. Hammond Trumbull published this 1870 study of place names drawn from the Algonkin languages of North America. Trumbull opens by rejecting the idea that a proper name is a mere mark with no meaning. In the native languages of America, he says, every name of a person or a place must keep the sense of its roots.

A name, on his account, must state its meaning with precision to all who speak the language. When sound change or changed circumstance strips a name of that self-defining power, the language drops it. The essay therefore reads place names as small pieces of grammar and history, and shows readers how to hear the meaning still held in them.
18472-the-amours-of-zeokinizul-king-of-t:
This little work presents itself as a translation from the Arabic of the famous traveller Krinelbol, with a key, printed in London for G. Smith near Temple Bar in 1749 at one shilling and sixpence. The preface insists that the translator has mixed nothing of his own into the amours of Zeokinizul, king of the Kofirans.

The book is a satirical romance of a king's loves, told as if from an eastern source, with a key inviting readers to match its characters to figures nearer home. Its charm lies in that game of disguise, where an exotic tale carries a sharp look at court life, love, and power in the author's own world.
1863-notes-on-a-journey-from-cornhill-to:
William Makepeace Thackeray's Notes on a Journey from Cornhill to Grand Cairo records his 1844 voyage from London to Egypt, by way of Vigo, Lisbon, Cadiz, Gibraltar, Athens, Smyrna, and Constantinople. The Lady Mary Wood carries him through the Mediterranean, and his chapters mix travel notes with satire on fellow passengers.

Thackeray watches card players quarrelling three hours before noon, armed to the teeth and afraid to fight. He notes that they are bred from the same land that begot philosophers and heroes. The book is travel writing with a novelist's eye, funny about hotels, guides, and ruins, and fond of the East even while it laughs at the tourist.
19217-the-history-of-england-in-three-vo:
Tobias Smollett continued David Hume's History of England in this second volume, from William and Mary to the death of George the Second. The 1860 edition carries maps of India, America, Scotland, and the Baltic, plus a front piece of Marlborough. Hume's first volume runs from Caesar to James the Second.

Smollett opens with the Convention turned into a Parliament, as William assures both houses he will guard their good opinion and tend Holland and the Protestant interest abroad. Appointments, parties, and wars follow in dense detail. Readers get a classic, if dated, narrative history of Britain's long eighteenth century.
19353-captain-jinks-hero:
Ernest Crosby wrote this satire of war fever, published in New York and London in the early nineteen hundreds, with pictures by Dan Beard. Sam Jinks, a schoolboy hero-worshiper, trains at a military academy, falls in love, and ships out to the Cubapines, a thin veil for Cuba and the Philippines. Each promotion feeds his hunger for glory.

Crosby's target is plain: a nation that turns soldiers into idols and war into business. Battles, dinners, and medals pile up until the hero's fame looks hollow. The novel still bites as a comedy of empire, written while American wars abroad were fresh news.
19800-london-and-the-kingdom-volume-1-a-:
Reginald R. Sharpe, the City of London's archivist, wrote London and the Kingdom. Volume one builds the history mainly from the City's own archives. Sharpe surveys what earlier writers covered: trade and craft guilds, for instance. He lists the powers of the Courts of Aldermen and Common Council. Church history, he notes, others handled well. His own ground is the City's records.

London's archives are among the richest any city keeps. Sharpe spent his career ordering and calendaring them. A history drawn from records corrects legend with paper. Guilds, courts, and the livery companies fill these pages. The book serves anyone tracing London's self-government. It is institutional history written by its keeper.
20990-london-and-the-kingdom-volume-2-a-:
Buckingham's murder, a forced loan, and four aldermen jailed crowd volume two's contents. Reginald Sharpe's London and the Kingdom draws its tale mainly from the City's own archives. The Long Parliament, Strafford, and Scottish envoys fill its Civil War years.

Sharpe, the City's records clerk, knew London's papers as few men did. Charters, letters, and council acts give his history its firm spine. Volume two runs from Charles the First to the Commonwealth's storms. Readers get London as a power in the land, proud, rich, and courted by kings and parliaments alike.
21206-the-romany-rye-a-sequel-to-lavengr:
George Borrow continues Lavengro in The Romany Rye, issued here in the 1900 Ward, Lock edition with an introduction by Theodore Watts-Dunton. Borrow opens with an advertisement answering critics who claimed Lavengro was cooked up against the popish agitation of 1850-51. He says the main part was written in 1843.

The sequel follows Borrow's wandering hero among gypsies, horse fairs, and roadside folk, mixing real travel with fiction. Romany language and lore run through it, as in Borrow's books on Spain. Its famous appendix defends his earlier work and attacks his critics. The title names a gypsy gentleman, which the hero in some sense becomes.
21380-a-young-hero:
Phil Carleton, eight or nine, sits over his Latin with grey, anxious Dr Martin. The French scholar in a black silk cap teaches him in George Manville Fenn's short tale. War between England and France is about to break over Canada, where they live. Phil's father, an English officer, suddenly arrives with hard orders.

The doctor must abandon his house, books, and papers at once and take the boy through hostile country to the English lines. Days of privation and insult from farmers follow, then arrest as supposed spies. In the end a battle comes, and the dying General Wolfe is brought drafts of water by young Phil himself.
22877-lavengro:
Scholar, Gypsy, and Priest walk through Lavengro, George Borrow's strange and famous book. Borrow warns readers on his title page not to merge the three figures into one. Something of the Gypsy may show in the Scholar, he grants. Nothing of the Priest shows in either, he insists.

Part novel, part memoir, the book follows a young word-lover through England and Wales. He learns Romany, boxes, tinkers, argues theology, and collects people the way others collect coins. Language itself is the real hero, with Gypsy speech honored throughout. Lavengro baffled and charmed its first readers in 1851. It still does both, and its road scenes remain among the most alive in English prose.
22878-lavengro:
Borrow's Lavengro continues in this second hosted portion of his roaming, bookish life. A voice in the excerpt muses on wishes and misery. The fulfilment of one's wishes, he has heard, is invariably the forerunner of extreme misery. A life without hope or wish, he adds, would be more horrible still.

That mix of road talk and reflection marks the whole work. Borrow drifts among Gypsies, priests, tinkers, and scholars, trading stories and arguments at every stop. Philology and fist fights sit comfortably side by side. Readers joining the book here should know it rewards wandering rather than plot. Taken slowly, the pages give a vanished England of lanes, fairs, and campfires, recorded by a man who loved its margins.
24785-nero:
Stephen Phillips published his verse play Nero in London and New York in 1906. The cast gathers the famous names of the early empire: Nero, his mother Agrippina, his half-brother Britannicus, Seneca, Burrus, Tigellinus, Octavia, and Poppaea. Years pass between acts as the young emperor slips from his mother's grip toward crime.

Phillips writes in blank verse, and the mother-son scenes carry the play: Agrippina reminds Nero who set him on the throne, and he answers that a kindness harped on grows an injury. Poison, spies, and court plots fill the later acts. The play offers a stately, poetic take on Rome's most notorious emperor.
25071-the-romany-rye-a-sequel-to-lavengr:
George Borrow's Romany Rye continues the wandering life story begun in Lavengro, following its narrator among Gypsy camps, horse dealers, and roadside acquaintances in England. The 1903 Methuen edition reprints Borrow's text with notes and an introduction by John Sampson.

Borrow writes in a loose, episodic style, mixing talk, anecdote, and scenes from the road rather than building a tight plot. Readers meet vivid minor figures and hear debates about language and belief. The book gives a firsthand-feeling portrait of travelling life in the mid-nineteenth century, told by a writer who lived close to the people he describes.
26507-the-future-of-the-american-negro:
Booker T. Washington's 1899 volume gathers his platform and magazine ideas on the future of Black Americans after slavery, in more definite and permanent form. Several pieces first appeared in the Atlantic Monthly and Appleton's Popular Science Monthly, and Washington thanks both journals for leave to reuse them. He writes from Tuskegee Normal and Industrial Institute, Alabama, in October 1899.

Chapters trace the first appearance of Black people in America, the Civil War, and Reconstruction, then argue that the whole country bears responsibility for their progress. Washington favors practical training over too much classical schooling at the start, and he closes on pride and faith in oneself as the ground of success. The book remains a key statement of his program.
27063-the-hero:
William Somerset Maugham's 1901 novel The Hero opens with Colonel Parsons by the window, finishing his Standard as the day fades. His wife knits a sock beside him, and outside stands a triumphal arch at the gate, built for the homecoming of their son, expected next day from South Africa.

The son returns from the Boer War to a village ready to celebrate him, but Maugham's hero finds the welcome harder than the war. The novel tests courage, reputation, and family pride, asking what a hero owes the people who made an arch for him.
28059-a-lost-hero:
Elizabeth Stuart Phelps Ward and Herbert D. Ward wrote A Lost Hero, published in Boston in 1893, as a story of a boy and a runaway horse. The tale opens at a small station, where a white boy tests a halter, a horse breaks away, and a crowd gives chase. Frank T. Merrill supplied the pictures.

What follows is a chain of small adventures: stray goats, a pauper dog, and an old man with torpedoes, all told with warmth and humour. The hero of the title is lost in more ways than one, and finding him tests the courage of those who search. Young readers get a brisk, old-fashioned tale of country life.
2812-letters-of-marcus-tullius-cicero:
This volume collects the surviving letters of Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator and statesman of the late Republic. Written to friends, family, and political allies, the letters cover elections, trials, exile, civil war, and the daily business of Roman life. They show Cicero arguing, worrying, and joking in his own voice rather than in the polished manner of his published speeches.

Readers gain a close view of Rome's last republican decades, including games with elephants that left crowds pitying the animals. The letters also reveal friendships and rivalries that shaped public decisions. The collection remains a central source for Roman history and a model of the familiar letter as a historical document.
28689-duncan-polite-the-watchman-of-glen:
Marian Keith wrote this 1905 Canadian novel about Duncan Polite, the watchman of the village of Glenoro. Duncan is an old, tall, stooped man living in a log shanty. The story follows his place in a close Presbyterian community, through covenants, Sabbaths, pastoral visits, a disastrous picnic, and the bursting of a storm. Chapters trace his despair, his acts of quiet kindness, and a covenant renewed.

Keith sets the tale among Ontario pioneers, where church, family, and neighborly duty shape every choice. The novel's warmth comes from its portraits of ordinary faithful people, including Jessie and Donald, and from Duncan's steady conscience. Readers get a gentle, old-fashioned story of a Scottish-Canadian village, written with sympathy for its plain, devout life.
30479-the-camerons-of-highboro:
Beth B. Gilchrist writes The Camerons of Highboro, copyrighted in 1919 and published in September of that year by the Century Company, with illustrations by Phillipps Ward. Gilchrist, author of Cinderella's Granddaughter, opens with Elliott planning and fate disposing, the end of a journey, and Cameron Farm.

Later chapters move through untrodden fields, a slacker unperceived, fliers, picnicking, a bee sting, and Elliott acting on an idea. Questions about a dress, a missing person, and home-loving hearts close the named scenes. A frontispiece shows how good bacon tasted when broiled on a forked stick. Gilchrist writes a warm farm and family tale for girls.
3114-the-education-of-the-negro:
Charles Dudley Warner wrote The Education of the Negro as an address on Black citizenship and schooling after emancipation. Warner notes that about five million Black people entered citizenship at the war's close, growing to over seven and a half million by the 1890 census. He uses the word negro as descriptive, distinguishing African peoples from other black or colored races such as Abyssinians.

Warner credits the race with humor, good humor, and capacity for devotion, testified by southerners during the Civil War, and argues those distinct traits might contribute to a cosmopolitan civilization. The address reflects its era's racial language and paternalism, while urging education as the path forward. It remains a document of post-Reconstruction debate over Black schooling.
31301-a-comparative-study-of-the-negro-p:
Charles C. Cook's 1899 paper, number four in the American Negro Academy's Occasional Papers, compares the Negro problem with the progress of nations. Cook argues that the thread of Black fate lies more in American hands than in Black hands. He turns to English history, where a restless people founded a faster civilization on this continent.

England, the United States, and Japan, he says, most startled the world by progress, yet what took England ten centuries took America two hundred years and Japan thirty. His answer in two words is machinery: England was chiefly hand-made, while America and above all Japan were made by machines. The paper is a striking turn-of-the-century argument about speed, industry, and destiny.
31366-a-little-dusky-hero:
Harriet T. Comstock's A Little Dusky Hero, published by Thomas Y. Crowell and Company with copyright in 1902, is a children's book lovingly dedicated by the author, as a mother, to Philip and Albert. Its first chapter introduces George Washington McKinley Jones, and later chapters bring a box from up North, a little gauntlet and sword, and a wait in a turret chamber. An illustration shows Colonel Austin staggering to his feet, leaning upon a little shoulder.

The story centers on a young hero whose courage matters more than his size. Comstock, author of Cedric the Saxon and Tower or Throne, writes for children in the sentimental, earnest style of her time. Modern readers will note the period language of the title while following a tale that praises bravery, loyalty, and a child's steady nerve.
31498-a-little-hero:
Mrs. Musgrave's A Little Hero was published by Blackie and Son of London, Glasgow, and Bombay in 1887. It is a children's story whose frontispiece shows Jeff learning of his coming journey to England. Musgrave, author of In Cloudland and The Lost Thimble, writes for young readers in the moral adventure tradition of the period. Jeff's journey to England, and the trials that follow, give the book its shape.

The hero of the title is a boy whose courage is tested away from home. Musgrave keeps the story short and direct, with clear lessons in bravery and steadiness. Readers of Victorian children's books will find a modest, well-meant tale, typical of the school and adventure stories Blackie published for boys and girls.
32564-twelve-times-zero:
Howard Browne's tale, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in March 1952, opens in a basement room where police grill a young man named Cordell. He moves with painful dignity, like a man on his way to a firing squad, hair rumpled, face gaunt and pale, forehead beaded with sweat under harsh light. Three hard men in ordinary clothes watch him, motioning him to a straight-backed chair in the centre of the room.

The case looks like a love-triangle murder making headlines, yet the tale's framing note says the answer lies hundreds of thousands of light years away. An illustration shows police grilling Cordell while eyes from a hundred worlds look on. Browne mixes a police interrogation with cosmic mystery, as a earthly crime opens onto watchers far beyond Earth.
32689-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, volume eight, runs alphabetically from Dinard to Dodsworth. It opens with Dinard, a seaside town in northwestern France and chief watering-place of Brittany, facing St. Malo across the mouth of the Rance.

Later articles cover dissection, Dindigul, dissenters, distillation, distress, districts, Diocletian and his edict, Diodorus, diptychs, and diving gear, among many more. Each entry gives the concise, scholarly treatment that made the eleventh edition famous, for readers seeking facts on arts, sciences, literature, and general knowledge. The slice serves as a handy reference for students, writers, and curious readers alike.
33110-corporal-lige-s-recruit-a-story-of:
James Otis's Corporal 'Lige's Recruit follows a young recruit in the French and Indian War country of the northern frontier. It is a story of Crown Point and Ticonderoga in the Young Patriot series and copyrighted in 1898. With six page illustrations by J. Watson Davis, the book gives young readers forts, soldiers, and the hard work of campaigning in the lake country between New York and Canada. The corporal of the title takes a raw recruit in hand.

Otis, a prolific writer for boys, tells history through a boy's eyes, mixing drill, danger, and humor with the facts of Crown Point and Ticonderoga. The story teaches the geography and stakes of a frontier war without losing its pace. It remains a lively period tale for young readers interested in American history, and a good example of the patriotic series books of its day.
33630-geological-report-on-asbestos-and-:
Lucius J. Boyd examines asbestos and its indications in the province of Quebec, Canada, in this 1889 geological report, with close attention to the eastern townships of Garthby, Wolfestown, and Coleraine. Boyd gave special attention to the distribution of asbestos-bearing serpentine rocks, which in his opinion had previously been only partially traced. Thick undergrowth in many places made penetration almost impossible, and months of heavy snowfall added further difficulty.

Earlier reports by R. E. Ellis, Dr. Hunt, and others on the origin and distribution of serpentines had been fully discussed, yet opinions still differed in many respects. The report aims to give a true account of the existence, location, and association of the asbestos rocks. For historians of Canadian mining and geology, it records an early, field-based effort to map a resource that would later become an industry.
35189-historical-romance-of-the-american:
Charles Fowler, a doctor, wrote this historical romance of the American negro, printed at Baltimore in 1902. In his preface he says the book had been on his mind for years: the agitation against slavery, the great Rebellion, and all that followed under freedom.

To make it readable he chose a representative woman of his race as mouthpiece, weaving the record into a tale of love and travel. The contents run twenty-two chapters, then turn to essays: Blacks in the Revolutionary War and in 1812, Nick Biddle, and Color Is No Bar to Office. Plates show the battles of Milliken's Bend and Port Hudson, John Brown, and Frederick Douglass. Readers get history carried by a heroine.
35592-some-current-folk-songs-of-the-neg:
Thomas wrote Some Current Folk-Songs of the Negro, a paper read before the Folk-Lore Society of Texas in 1912 and later reprinted by the society. Thomas taught English for nearly thirty years at the Agricultural and Mechanical College of Texas. His pamphlet was the first item the young society ever produced.

Thomas held that folklore workers should not only collect lore but interpret it and enjoy it too. Society dues of two bits a year long kept publication thin, the reprint note explains with humour. Songs current among Black singers in Texas form the heart of the pamphlet, set down with notes. Folklore students get an early Texas collection and a humane collecting creed.
35770-the-hero:
The Hero is a science fiction story by Elaine Wilber, drawn with art by Paul Orban. Wilber opens with a dry note that Willy was a hero for sure, though which side he served is hard to say. The tale is set on a far world named Engraham.

Two months after landing, the ship UXB-69311 has been refit to feel more like a country club than a barracks. The crew, with leave from Colonel Mondrain, turned part of the bunk room into a calm, smart bar. When the crew first landed, the local folk fled, then came back in peace. A crew man named O Connors first found a good fruit on near bushes. Wilber builds a wry tale of ease, trade, and blurred sides on a new world.
38556-historic-waterways-six-hundred-mil:
Reuben Gold Thwaites wrote Historic Waterways, six hundred miles of canoeing down the Rock, Fox, and Wisconsin rivers, for McClurg of Chicago in 1888. Thwaites served as secretary of the State Historical Society of Wisconsin. He gives the book to his wife, his messmate on two of the three vacation voyages told here.

His preface scolds the common run of holiday makers, who rush far off for rest and learn less of their own state than of any other. Take a canoe instead, he says, and work the nearest river from source to mouth. A line from Thoreau heads the title page: the river steals into the scenery it crosses, free to come and go as the breeze.
39448-twelve-years-of-a-soldier-s-life-i:
Twelve Years of a Soldier's Life in India gathers extracts from the letters of the late Major W S R Hodson. His brother, the Rev George H Hodson, edited them. Ticknor and Fields published the Boston edition in 1860, from the third enlarged English edition. Hodson served in the First Bengal European Fusileers. He commanded the irregular cavalry remembered as Hodson's Horse.

The letters include a personal narrative of the Siege of Delhi. The capture of the King and Princes forms its climax. A Fraser's Magazine paper by the author of Tom Brown's School Days opens the volume. It recalls England's agony during the rebellion of 1857. Week after week, readers waited for scanty despatches from the Northwest Provinces. Then came tales of a little band turning to bay. Hodson stood foremost among the heroes.
41163-master-wace-his-chronicle-of-the-n:
Edgar Taylor Englished Master Wace chronicle of the Norman Conquest from French verse. Pickering printed the book in London in 1837 with plates. Taylor gives the book to Hudson Gurney in respect and regard. Plates draw on the Bayeux Tapestry and old manuscripts for scenes.

Chapter one tells how William became duke and his barons revolted. The King of France came, and battle raged at Val des Dunes. Canute death, Alfred fall by treason, and Edward crown follow next. William of Arques revolt and the Mortemer fight fill later chapters. Edgar Taylor turned the verse chronicle into English prose.
41245-a-guide-to-the-virginia-springs-gi:
A small guide to the Virginia springs was printed at Staunton in 1851, put out by Robert Cowan. Its preface says no portable guide to these watering places had yet appeared. The compiler drew on the spring owners and on earlier books.

Routes come first, with distances stage by stage from Washington City. One road runs down the Potomac, by rail to Charlottesville, then by stage through Staunton. The book then describes each spring and the natural sights of the state, such as Monticello. It was made for health seekers planning a summer trip. Distances are given mile by mile, so a traveller could plan each day's stage with care.
41399-admirals-of-the-british-navy-portr:
Admirals of the British Navy is a portrait book with paintings by Francis Dodd. Country Life and George Newnes published it in London in 1917. An introduction and biographical notes accompany the colour portraits. The contents list the admirals in order of seniority. Jellicoe, the fleet commander, stands first among them. Burney and Madden follow in the contents list. Phillimore, Bacon, and de Robeck come next in turn. Napier, Brock, and Halsey fill the later numbers.

The book appeared while the Great War was still being fought. Its portraits honour the Royal Navy's wartime leaders in colour. Dodd painted officers of the Grand Fleet and its stations. Biographical notes give each man's service in brief. The volume is a patriotic gallery of the sea war. Country Life issued it from its Tavistock Street offices.
44705-mammals-collected-by-dr-w-l-abbott:
Mammals Collected by Abbott on the Natuna Islands is a paper by Gerrit Miller. It appeared in the Proceedings of the Washington Academy of Sciences in March 1901. The specimens went to the United States National Museum.

Abbott spent about three months of 1900 exploring the islands in the South China Sea. He worked seven islands, from Pulo Midei in May to Pulo Laut in August. About two hundred and sixty-five mammals were obtained for the museum. Earlier collectors, Everett in 1893 and Hose in 1894, had recorded twenty-eight land mammals. Abbott secured forty-four species, though he missed seven of the earlier ones. The islands' total thus rose to fifty-one species. Miller weighs whether the fauna leans toward Borneo or toward the Malay Peninsula.
4516-peter-a-novel-of-which-he-is-not-th:
F. Hopkinson Smith tells this novel through a friend who watches Peter, a bank clerk poring over his ledger late one December afternoon. Peter, bald and grey-browed, has kept the same walk uptown with the narrator for years, and the sight of him still at his desk after four o'clock signals trouble. The title warns readers at once that Peter, for all his presence, is not quite the hero of his own tale.

Through bank work, friendships, and quiet acts of character, Smith builds a warm portrait of an ordinary man caught in larger events. The narrator's fond, observant voice gives the book its charm, as small daily habits reveal loyalty, worry, and decency. Readers get a gentle American novel about friendship and work, where the most interesting man in the room is not always the one who drives the plot.
45667-the-boy-scouts-along-the-susquehan:
Herbert Carter wrote this Boy Scouts adventure, copyrighted in 1915, with the full title The Boy Scouts Along the Susquehanna, or The Silver Fox Patrol Caught in a Flood. Carter wrote many other scout tales, from The Boy Scouts' First Campfire to The Boy Scouts in the Rockies. The story opens with Davy warning the boys that heavy rain is on its way.

Chapter titles trace the patrol's trip toward the river and into danger. The boys camp in a haymow, shelter in a deserted shanty boat, and end up adrift on the flood. Later chapters turn to signs, a marauder's trail, and a capture, before the patrol heads for home in the last chapter.
45759-london-and-the-kingdom-volume-3-a-:
London and the Kingdom, volume three, is a history drawn from city archives. Reginald Sharpe, records clerk at Guildhall, built the work from those papers. The Corporation of the City of London ordered the printing of it. Longmans, Green brought the three volumes out in the year 1895. This last volume runs from the accession of George the First.

Jacobite rebellion, the Old Pretender, and impeached ministers open the tale. The Septennial Act and the trial of the Earl of Oxford follow. The South Sea Company and Walpole's rise fill the next long chapter. Jenkin's ear, war with Spain, and the taking of Porto Bello come on. The Young Pretender, Black Friday, and Culloden crowd the mid volume. Sharpe tells national events through the City's own kept records. Writs and returns stand copied in facsimile at the book's front.
45871-a-fleet-in-being-notes-of-two-trip:
Rudyard Kipling wrote A Fleet in Being, notes of two Channel Squadron trips. Macmillan issued the 1914 form at London. The book first came out in December 1898. Reprints ran through 1899, 1910, and 1914. Some thirty men-of-war shared the matter, he says. A dozen battleships of the newest kind stood among them.

Seventeen or eighteen cruisers filled out the fleet. Kipling's concern was one new-type cruiser alone. An old friend of his commanded her then. He stepped from a Portsmouth wherry one summer evening. The year was 1897 in his telling. None aboard topped twenty-eight years but the captain. The chief engineer and a few petty officers shared that rank. Young gentlemen ran the light 20-knot ship. A poet afloat with the fleet gives the modern navy a face of bright, keen boys.
46293-germany-s-dishonoured-army-additio:
Germany's Dishonoured Army presents additional records of German atrocities in France, by Professor J H Morgan. Morgan had been a home office commissioner with the British expeditionary force. The pamphlet was issued in nineteen fifteen by a parliamentary recruiting committee. A note at its head tells how the inquiry was made. In November nineteen fourteen Morgan was commissioned to investigate alleged breaches of the laws of war in France, it says.

His work extended over four or five months, the note goes on. Six weeks were spent in base hospitals and camps at Boulogne, Rouen, and Paris. The remaining months he was attached to general headquarters. He questioned some two or three thousand officers and soldiers in person, it says. They came from almost every regiment and had lately been in the field.
46323-the-soul-of-the-soldier-sketches-f:
Thomas Tiplady, a chaplain to the forces and author of The Cross at the Front, wrote The Soul of the Soldier as sketches from the Western battle-front. Fleming Revell Company issued the book in 1918 at New York and London. He gave it to the memory of men he had known in the London Territorials, who went over the parapet and did not return. A plate shows Captain Guy Drummond of the 13th Royal Canadian Highlanders, killed in action in 1915.

A poem at the front, The Mother's Answer by James Hughes, gives a mother's voice to the grief. She holds her son gave himself to save all a Christian should revere, and that God's test of manhood is not whether he came back but whether he went. Tiplady's sketches draw the inner life of the common soldier at the front.
46386-the-castaways-of-pete-s-patch-a-se:
Carroll Watson Rankin wrote The Castaways of Pete's Patch for Henry Holt, as a sequel to The Adopting of Rosa Marie in her Dandelion Cottage series. Ada Williamson illustrated it, and Miriam Selss drew the frontispiece and jacket.

The publisher's jacket copy invites the reader in. How many girls have wished to spend a summer in a real camp on the shores of a lake? Soft grass kind to bare feet, camp beds of fragrant balsam tips, and plenty of real adventure are promised. Here the friends of Dandelion Cottage are marooned on a point of land. Indian boys, a castaway sailor lad, and many other happenings fill the book. Rankin wrote from Michigan's Upper Peninsula, and her cottage girls were local heroines. The series ran for years on this recipe: a lake, a summer, and girls competent at both.
48771-roman-legends-a-collection-of-the-:
Roman Legends, a collection of the fables and folk-lore of Rome, was gathered by R H Busk and printed at Boston in 1877. Busk also wrote Sagas from the Far East and Household Stories from the Land of Hofer. In the preface Busk says it was often flatly asserted that modern Italy had no popular mythology to offer the world's store of tales.

Possessing every chance to test the claim, Busk long shrank from trying. A humble friend at last convinced Busk that she might be a rich store of such lore if it existed. Examining her proved the point. One tale she gave was of Saint Giovanni Bocca d'oro, with two stories of Padre Filippo. Her testimony on the crucifix of Scirollo also came in usefully. The book prints the legends of the Roman people in English.
48897-famous-frontiersmen-and-heroes-of-:
Famous Frontiersmen and Heroes of the Border is a collective biography by Charles Johnston, published in Boston by Page in 1913. It belongs to his Famous Leaders series, beside volumes on cavalry leaders, Indian chiefs, scouts, and privateersmen. Daniel Morgan's portrait appears at the front.

The subtitle promises adventurous lives and stirring experiences in pioneer days. Johnston says requests for more tales followed his earlier Famous Scouts. Each life is told as a story of marches, fights, and escapes on the American border. The series sold at a dollar fifty a volume, large and illustrated, for boys and general readers. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
50585-a-thousand-degrees-below-zero:
Murray Leinster printed A Thousand Degrees Below Zero in The Thrill Book of July 15, 1919, and the opening is a small masterpiece of strangeness. A musical humming grows overhead, not the rasp of an aeroplane motor, and a cold breeze beats down on the Coney Island steamer, actively, actually cold.

The passengers joke about drafts and cold shoulders while the temperature falls out of the summer sky. Leinster, who wrote science fiction for sixty years, loved a physical impossibility pursued with logic: something above the steamer is making cold, a thousand degrees below zero by the title's cheerful arithmetic. The Thrill Book folded within the year; the story's chill outlasted the magazine.
51267-end-as-a-hero:
End as a Hero is a tale of the stars by Keith Laumer. Schelling made its plates. The host text was made from a sheet of tale writ of the past age. Its bill word gives the theme in one line: the task of its hero was the most live of the war. It would mean a swift win, but for whom, that word asks. The tale is told in the first voice.

In the dream I was swim in a stream of white fire, the tale starts. The dream went on and on with no end. Then I was awake, and the fire was still there. It burnt at me with fierce heat past the dream. I tried to move to get past the flames, and then the true pain hit.
52059-anthologica-rarissima-the-way-of-a:
Anthologica Rarissima is a privately printed anthology of excerpts from rare and curious books, issued in London in 1922 for members of the Brovan Society. Two hundred and fifty copies were printed on hand-made paper for private circulation only, and none was for sale. The Society pledged never to reprint the work.

The first volume is titled The Way of a Virgin. The editors present the series as research into the less-known and more curious folk-lore and literature of Europe and the Orient. Some pieces appear in English for the first time. Copious notes and bibliographical references serve the student, the collector, and the psychologist, the title page says. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
52694-st-paul-the-hero:
Rufus Jones wrote a life of Saint Paul for young readers, printed in New York in 1917 with pictures and maps. Jones had written The Inner Life. A picture of Tarsus fronts the book. The first chapter shows Paul as a boy of ten years, and his boyhood heroes follow.

Chapters move through Jerusalem, Rabbi Gamaliel's school, and tent making in Tarsus. The great teacher of Galilee, the man with a shining face, and the road to Damascus turn the tale. Missionary journeys, a letter to his churches, a call to Macedonia, Athens, Corinth, prison at Caesarea, and a stormy voyage to Rome fill the rest. Paul stands as hero of faith and grit for boys and girls.
54001-il-nipotismo-di-roma-or-the-histor:
Il Nipotismo di Roma, the History of the Popes' Nephews, was printed in London in sixteen sixty-nine for John Starkey at the Miter near Temple-Bar. The work first appeared in Italian in sixteen sixty-seven and was Englished by a translator who signed only initials. Its span runs from Sixtus the Fourth to the death of the last pope, Alexander the Seventh, across two parts.

The hosted text was transcribed from the Starkey edition, keeping the spelling and grammar of sixteen sixty-nine as printed. In his address to the reader, the author gives two plain reasons for skipping the usual ceremonies of a preface. He will not make excuses before knowing if anyone wants them, and ceremony looks wrong before so many practiced flatterers.
54048-the-romany-rye-a-sequel-to-lavengr:
George Borrow's sequel to Lavengro, first published in 1857, appears here in John Murray's London edition of 1907, with the text unaltered and notes added. Borrow's own advertisement of 1857 answers a printed charge that Lavengro was got up against the popish agitation of 1850 and 1851. He replies that most of that book was written in 1843 and the whole finished before the end of 1846.

He adds that the manuscript was in the publisher's hands in 1848, and that the publisher should have rebutted the charge himself. Borrow says he has no cause to be ashamed of the book and some cause to be proud of it. The volume opens its front matter with the tale of Cogia Efendy, scorned at a feast for his old dress and honored when he returns in a splendid pelisse.
54082-the-new-map-of-europe-1911-1914-th:
Herbert Adams Gibbons wrote this account of how Europe slid into the Great War. The Century Company printed The New Map of Europe at New York in 1916, and it ran through four editions in a year. Gibbons had written on the founding of the Ottoman Empire.

His span is 1911 to 1914: the talks, crises, and small wars that redrew the map. A map of the Balkan lands in 1914 fronts the book. Germany in Alsace and Lorraine opens the tale. Gibbons gave the book to his three children, born in Adana, Constantinople, and Paris amid the wars. May they lead lives of peace, he writes, in the gift page.
55774-the-law-of-storms-the-various-phen:
Captain John Ross compiled The Law of Storms from various sources, and Roman and Company published it in San Francisco in 1869. Its full title promises the phenomena by which a storm's approach can be known with certainty, and practical directions to mariners for avoiding its fury. Two San Francisco trade advertisements precede the title page in this copy.

The opening chapter states the law of storms through Dove's law of gyration, the regular rotation of winds in each hemisphere. Ross explains how the earth's rotation bends polar and equatorial currents of air, and how the trade winds and monsoons follow from that bending. The mariner's rules grow out of these shifts of wind round the compass.
55842-the-pennsylvania-journal-of-prison:
The Pennsylvania Journal of Prison Discipline and Philanthropy, volume eight number two, is the April 1853 number of a quarterly. It cost one dollar a year in advance. The Philadelphia Society for Alleviating the Miseries of Public Prisons, founded in 1787, directed it. Biddle printed it at Philadelphia, and Gilpin sold it at London.

An epigraph states the society's creed: separating one prisoner from another is the only sound basis of reforming discipline. Articles treat moral instruction of convicts and English convict prisons. Others ask whether convicts should enter the state lunatic hospital at Harrisburg. Notices cover vagrant children, street begging, and new penitentiaries. The journal argues the separate system to America.
56276-the-comical-pilgrim-or-travels-of-:
The Comical Pilgrim is a merry satire of the age, in a second London form dated 1722. Its hero is a cynic thinker who tours what the title page calls the most wicked parts of the world: England, Ireland, Wales, Scotland, and Holland. He is no grave pilgrim bound for a shrine, but a laughing rider out to see how folk live.

His notes mock the English stage, gaming houses, poets, beaux, courtiers, and plotters. Welsh clergy and customs, Scots manners and lawyers, and Irish rites at weddings, christenings, and burials all get their turn. Dutch rule, policy, and trade close the tour. The whole is a broad laugh at vice and folly, in the loose spelling of its day.
56294-historical-record-of-the-twelfth-o:
Historical Record of the Twelfth, or the Prince of Wales's, Regiment belongs to a series of regimental histories of the British Army. A general order from the Horse Guards, dated January eighteen thirty six, opens the book. The king had commanded, it says, that an account of the services of every regiment be published. The Adjutant General was to direct the work.

The order sets out what each account must hold. Formation of the regiment and its stations come first. Battles, sieges, and other operations follow, with any trophies taken from the enemy. Names of officers and men killed or wounded must be given, with place and date. Officers honoured for gallant service are to be named as well. The order argues that the army's credit rests on the zeal of those who serve in it.
56369-coward-or-hero:
Coward or Hero is a boys' story translated from the French by Sale Barker. George Routledge published it in London in 1884. It carries twenty-five illustrations in the original printing. The book belongs to a uniform series of adventure tales for boys.

The young narrator tells the story in the first person. Chapter titles sketch his scrapes and terrors as they come. A captain's anger, a colonel's system of training, and good resolutions open the tale. A monster sighting and a creature named Frimousse follow close behind. A horse called Montézuma and a bogey named Croquemitaine haunt the middle chapters. Daring exploits and a proud little bantam crowd the later pages. The question of the title hangs over the boy throughout. Each scare tests whether he is the coward he fears or something braver.
56625-songs-of-the-west-folk-songs-of-de:
Songs of the West gathers folk songs of Devon and Cornwall, collected from the mouths of the people. Baring-Gould, Fleetwood Sheppard, and Bussell made the collection. Cecil Sharp served as musical editor. Methuen published the fifth edition in one volume at London. The songs first appeared in four parts in 1890, and in one volume in 1892.

A revised edition followed in 1905, and this printing is dated April 1913. The collectors dedicate the book to the memory of Radford of Mount Tavy. At his hospitable table the making of the collection was first planned. They also honour Sheppard, a fellow worker in the field for twelve years. The contents run from the Sprig of Thyme to Widdecombe Fair. John Barleycorn, the Helston Furry Dance, Henry Martyn, and the Golden Vanity stand among them.
56908-the-pennsylvania-journal-of-prison:
April 1849 brings volume IV, number II, of a quarterly on prisons put out in Philadelphia for one dollar a year. E C and J Biddle printed the journal for the Philadelphia Society for Alleviating the Miseries of Public Prisons. That society dates to 1787, and its charter opens the number.

Three main essays treat houses of refuge, deaths and crime, and state penitentiaries in turn. Short notices then sweep the field: asylums for the insane, truancy counts in Boston, and a shelter for coloured orphans. One note asks if holding convicts apart from each other breeds ill health or madness, a live point in the separate system debate. Reports from Kentucky and Cincinnati add fresh counts from the ground.
56972-light-ahead-for-the-negro:
Light Ahead for the Negro, by Johnson, author of a school history of the Negro race, was copyrighted in 1904 and published in New York by the Grafton Press. The tale is framed as a vision in ten chapters. They run from The Lost Airship through To Earth Again, One Hundred Years Later. Visits to a public library, public buildings, and a young ladies' guild follow, ending with a prize essay.

The narrator says his father was an abolitionist before the war and a backer of mission work in the South. He himself resolved in young manhood to spend his life among Black Southerners. His aim was to help fit them for the new citizenship the war had brought. A Yale course kept the resolve firm. The flight and the century leap let Johnson picture the progress he hoped to see.
57094-the-autobiography-of-lieutenant-ge:
The life tale of Sir Harry Smith, a British chief of war, was first put out in nineteen one. Smith wrote the tale of his own life from his birth year to eighteen forty-six. An kin hand then adds parts on his last years to eighteen sixty. The book came out in two parts, then in one part two years on.

Smith began his writ at Glasgow in eighteen twenty-four, then took it up past twenty years past in India with great speed. Half the tale covers his youth, when he saw war on two main lands with small charge. Past eighteen twenty-nine the scene shifts to two far main lands, and his charge grew vast. That shift marks the tone of the two halves.
57156-the-scarecrow-or-the-glass-of-trut:
The Scarecrow, or the Glass of Truth, is a stage play by Percy MacKaye, subtitled a tragedy of the ludicrous. MacKaye, a leading American dramatist of his generation, built the piece as a morality in which comedy and judgment share the stage. The printed text preserves the antiquated spellings of its period dress and marks each act with its own full heading.

The edition also states the terms of performance at length: all rights, professional and amateur, are reserved, and public performance without consent carries damages under the copyright statutes. That legal care reflects MacKaye's standing in the movement for a serious American theatre. The play itself, part farce and part reckoning, asks what a hollow figure propped up as a gentleman is truly worth.
57319-san-isidro:
Crowninshield wrote this tale, printed at Chicago and New York in 1900. Don Beltran keeps his house down by the river, though his neighbours warn him that a flood greater than any yet known will one day sweep house and inmates to the sea. He laughs at them. He is happy and content as he is.

His cacao and bananas stand on gentle rises the water has never reached, and the cattle always make for the grove on the hill. Once a cloudburst caught him with his serving-man Adan and Adan's niece Agueda, and the horses had gone. The tale settles into that lush, dangerous river world, where ease and peril share one roof and the flood is only ever a season away.
57400-rambles-in-istria-dalmatia-and-mon:
Rambles in Istria, Dalmatia and Montenegro is a travel book signed only R H R, published in London by Hurst and Blackett in 1875. Its preface answers the yearly question, where shall we go this summer, by pointing off the beaten track. The countries named lie within easy reach of London, seldom visited, cheap, and safe.

The road runs through Vienna and Pesth first, with cathedrals, the Danube, and the Universal Exhibition. Then come Trieste, the Karst, and a flying visit to San Canziano, where a mountain stream runs underground. Earthquake shocks at Belluno and an Austrian ironclad named Lissa season the Adriatic chapters. The author promises new scenery and fresh impressions for travellers tired of the old grand tour, at moderate expense and with total freedom from danger.
5816-successful-exploration-through-the-:
Successful Exploration Through the Interior of Australia recounts a great overland journey, opening with a biographical sketch of birth, infancy, boyhood, education, and youthful traits. A second chapter sends two sons from England to Australia, with voyage incidents, journal extracts, arrival at Port Phillip, and Melbourne life. Shepherd work in the interior, Melbourne in 1853, and advice to immigrants follow.

Readers follow explorers from home to outback, through stations, deserts, and the slow work of mapping a continent. The book blends biography, journal, and practical guidance, giving a full picture of colonial Australia in the 1850s. It suits readers of exploration history and Australian history, offering a detailed, firsthand-flavored account of a famous interior crossing.
58898-from-paddington-to-penzance-the-re:
A road walker records a tramp in From Paddington to Penzance, the record of a summer tramp from London to Cornwall. The front pages sell the book by its elder brother, The Brighton Road, old times and new on a classic highway. That volume had ninety illustrations, and long press notices are quoted for it.

The revived interest in our long neglected highways, one notice says, has produced a crop of books of English road life and scenery. Few have been more attractive than this volume, it holds. The author has gathered much amusing matter, chiefly on coaching and life on the road in the days of George the Fourth. He sets it beside his own observations and adventures on the way. The same love of the road drives this longer walk west.
59026-the-pennsylvania-journal-of-prison:
The Philadelphia Society for Alleviating the Miseries of Public Prisons puts out its quarterly in volume seven, number three, for July 1852. E C and J Biddle print the journal at Fifth and Minor Streets in Philadelphia, at one dollar a year in advance. A motto holds that separation of prisoners is the sole sound base for reform in prison rule.

Five articles fill the number, from an obituary of John Haviland to a report on a new gaol for Suffolk County. Dr Given's report on the Pennsylvania system, juvenile delinquency, and insane convicts fill the middle heads. Short notices then sweep foreign and home news: crime, pauperism, asylums, and prisons from Perth to Rhode Island in brief lines.
59405-pee-wee-harris-f-o-b-bridgeboro:
Percy Keese Fitzhugh sends a scout home in Pee Wee Harris, F O B Bridgeboro, printed in New York with copyright in 1923. Grosset and Dunlap made the book, published with the approval of the Boy Scouts of America. Barbour draws the plates. Fitzhugh had writ the Tom Slade books and the Roy Blakeley books. A frontispiece shows Pee Wee reaching out a leg to get a foot hold.

Twenty two chapters of small adventures follow. The only original and the fateful gum drop lead. Another inspiration, chaos and confusion, and northward bound fill the early run. Enter Lizzie and adventures with a flivver bring a car into camp life. A scout is polite, up in the air, and first aid vary the days. Pee Wee does not watch his step gets a chapter of warning. The panic, suspense, and the scout close in.
60972-a-practical-hand-book-of-drawing-f:
Charles Harper's A Practical Handbook of Drawing for Modern Methods of Reproduction was published by Chapman and Hall at London in 1894. Harper wrote English Pen Artists of To-Day. The title page keeps the original's Roman v for u in Reprodvction, as the transcriber notes. The book is illustrated with drawings by several hands and Harper's own sketches showing comparative results from the several reproduction methods in use.

A long, joking dedication to editor Charles Morley recalls the Pall Mall Budget's early picture-making from type: brass rules for rivers, asterisks for mountain chains. Process illustration, Harper says, owes its news position to Morley's chair. The preface opens on the illustrator's ubiquity: everywhere today is the illustrator, artist he may not always be. The handbook serves working pen artists facing the new photo-mechanical processes.
61620-the-mark-of-zorro:
Johnston McCulley wrote The Mark of Zorro, a tale of California, issued at New York by Grosset and Dunlap with a 1924 copyright. He gave the book to Douglas Fairbanks, the first Zorro of the screen. Its thirty-nine chapters run from Pedro the Boaster through sword clashes, a whipping, swift punishment, and flight and pursuit, to the man unmasked.

The tale opens on a night of rain and wind at a tavern, where Sergeant Pedro Gonzales warms his feet at the fire, wine in hand. He calls it a night for evil deeds. Against the fat and boastful sergeant stands the masked Señor Zorro, who rides for the poor against the proud. Idle Don Diego, who seeks a bride, hides more than he shows. McCulley's tale set the fox sign, the mask, and the blade work that films made famous.
62451-emperor-william-first-the-great-wa:
George Upton turned this life of Emperor William the First from the German of A Walter, and it came out at Chicago in 1909. The book belongs to a series of life stories for young people. Four prints face the text. It traces William from a frail child to the first emperor of a united Germany.

William won the Iron Cross as a youth and served in the last wars against Napoleon. Hated in the revolt year of 1848, he later won all hearts in the war with France in 1870. Chapters cover the wars with Austria and France, army tales, home life, and his death. Bismarck and Von Moltke stand beside him as the men who made Germany strong.
63113-the-lathe-of-morpheus-or-the-dream:
Printed privately at Bournemouth in 1915, a long poem in six parts pays tribute to a woman the verse calls Bridget. The first part is an invocation, begging that memory not hide the loved face behind grey curtains. Bridget is hailed as unreal, a dead phantom, yet living and breathing.

Later parts move through the Garden of Sleep and the leaden table, then close with an apologia to Bridget. Three short pieces follow, two songs and a sonnet to a bowl of gold and scarlet tulips. The verse is dense with dream, sleep, and death images. It reads as a private act of mourning, printed for a few.
63297-the-brother-of-a-hero:
The Brother of a Hero is a school story by Ralph Henry Barbour. Appleton published it in New York and London in 1914. Charles Relyea drew the illustrations. A shelf of Barbour's earlier school tales stands listed at the front.

The hero is Rodney Merrill, who arrives by steamer as the tale opens. He clutches a brand-new suitcase and his ticket as the boat nears the wharf. Chapters show him climbing a hill, meeting twins, and finding his school. Coach Cotting exacts a promise from him early in his time there. Reflected glory, the title's burden, is named in a chapter of its own. Rodney joins the football squad and survives the final cut of players.
63416-rust-smut-mildew-mould-an-introduc:
Rust, Smut, Mildew, and Mould is an introduction to tiny fungi by Cooke. Hardwicke of London issued this third edition in 1872. Nearly three hundred figures by Sowerby aid the text. Cooke had written a plain account of British fungi before. A new appendix lists finds made since 1865. The orders treated are the small plant diseases. Rusts redden wheat, and smuts blacken grain.

Mildews coat leaves, and moulds spoil stored food. Such fungi were then barely understood by farmers. Cooke writes for growers and amateur men of science. His index of British fungi served as a check list. He helped found the study of fungi in Britain. This little book stayed in print for years.
6391-the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-vol:
Two celebrated families, Calvini and Aenobarbi, spring from the race of the Domitii, and Nero belongs to the second, Suetonius begins. The Aenobarbi take name and descent from Lucius Domitius. Met on his road to Rome by two young men of august appearance, he was bidden to announce a victory not yet known in the city. To prove themselves more than mortal, they stroked his cheeks and turned his black hair bright as brass, a mark passed to his posterity.

Nero Claudius Caesar's life, in Thomson's translation revised by Forester, runs from that omen to an emperor's reign of informers, treason charges, and Greek crowns demanded as equivalents. Lawyers who drew wills for a prince's profit faced fines, and purple colours were forbidden to others while agents bought in secret. Suetonius writes Nero as a prince whose art and cruelty both became law.
64515-synthetic-hero:
Erik Fennel wrote the science fiction story Synthetic Hero, first printed in Planet Stories in the fall of 1948. Its subject is George Carlin, a rich industrialist who, in the story's own blurb, trampled his way to power and then bought a one-way ticket to the Moon to win undying gratitude. A statue of him stands at Southwestern Spaceport, and crowds visit it in silence.

The narrator undercuts the shrine at once: history, he says, is a fabric of accepted lies. The statue's plaque praises sacrifice and the conquest of disease, but the true shrine is a blasted circle of wreckage on the Moon. Carlin, spoiled and selfish for all his thirty-six years, thought of a spaceship only after catching the incurable Matson's Disease — as the most showy form of suicide ever devised. Readers get a sour tale of fame built on a lie.
65004-the-alhambra-and-the-kremlin-the-s:
A travel volume by Samuel Irenaeus Prime, published at New York in 1873. Anson D F Randolph issued the book. Prime also wrote Travels in Europe and the East. His plan contrasts Europe's south and north. The Alhambra stands as the south's type. The Kremlin symbolises the north. Both are fortresses enclosing palaces, he writes.

No formal comparison of morals and manners is attempted. Candid description instead gives life as it is in Spain and Scandinavia. Since the journey, Spain's queen had fled and France's emperor had fallen. Social life, Prime insists, remains the same across ages. The Generaliffe gardens form the frontispiece. Burgos, the Escorial, Madrid, and Toledo illustrate the Spanish road. The northern half turns to Russia and Scandinavia.
65050-brief-for-the-higher-education-of-:
Brief for the Higher Education of the Negro, a pamphlet by Professor Kelly Miller of Howard University, was published at Washington in 1903. Miller argues the case for college training for Black Americans. He writes against a climate of ridicule and contempt toward Black striving after learning.

The opening pages state the view he fights. The African, he says, was brought to America for manual and menial labour, and his worth is still measured by bodily powers alone. Thinkers from Carlyle down are shown holding that servitude is his ordained place. Miller answers that the higher powers of mind and soul were denied only because they were not wanted. His brief pleads that they be trained and used.
65160-the-discoveries-of-john-lederer-in:
The Discoveries of John Lederer is an early account of travel into the American interior. It was printed in London in 1672 for the bookseller Samuel Heyrick. William Talbot collected the text and translated it out of Latin. A general map of the whole territory traversed accompanies the discourse.

Lederer's three marches ran from Virginia westward toward Carolina. They began in March 1669 and ended in September 1670. The dedication addresses Lord Ashley, a lord proprietor of Carolina. From this discourse, it argues, a great discovery nearly approaches. The long looked-for Indian Sea, a western ocean, seems within reach. The Appalachian mountains, like a wall, deny Virginia passage westward. Yet they stoop, the dedication claims, toward Carolina's dominions instead. A prospect into unlimited empires opens beyond them in that hope. The little book is a foundation text of southern exploration.
66052-florida-trails-as-seen-from-jackso:
Winthrop Packard wrote a nature travel book on Florida, held under copyright in 1910, with photos by himself and others. He gives the book to his mother and thanks Florida folk for warm welcome and guidance on the road. Parts first ran in a Boston paper, whose editors let him reprint them here in book form.

The route runs from Jacksonville to Key West through the months from November to April. Chapters go south with the warblers, watch southern butterflies, and walk river margins at dawn. Christmas at St Augustine, a Florida freeze, the Indian River, seven thousand pelicans, and orange and grapefruit groves fill the middle chapters of the trip.
66249-the-hunter-hercules-or-the-champio:
The Hunter Hercules, or The Champion Rider of the Plains, is a romance of the prairies by Harry St. George, a writer for Beadle and Adams of New York. The story was entered for copyright in 1872. Twenty short chapters promise a circus rider magician, two wizards, and a trial of speed for scalps.

The scene opens on a bright October morning in the Lone Star State, near the Comanche ground on the northwestern border of Texas. A young hunter of about twenty two rides across the baked brown prairie in a fine buckskin suit. Ralph, as later chapters name him, wears a large felt hat and carries vast strength in a well knit frame, and his big bay horse was chosen for speed.
67214-the-book-of-history-vol-1-of-18-a-:
Volume one of The Book of History opens a history of all nations from the earliest times to the present. Viscount Bryce wrote the introduction. More than eight thousand illustrations fill the set. A front picture shows the saurian age, when gigantic reptiles ruled the world. Scholars from many lands share the work.

Flinders Petrie, Lane Poole, Sayce, and Alfred Russel Wallace stand in the author list. Volume one is named Man and the Universe, and starts with the world before history. It tells the story of the earth from the first thing known of it to the present time. Man's story follows the same vast arc, from first traces to modern thought.
67548-history-of-a-world-of-immortals-wi:
History of a World of Immortals Without a God is a tale of an imagined world by Antares Skorpios, printed at Dublin in 1891.
