The title page claims it was translated from an unpublished manuscript in the library of a continental university. The first chapter tells of Gervaas Van Varken, a doctor who loathed the whole human race.

Van Varken meets an old Parsee merchant in Bombay and wins a way to the great magician of Thibet. There he learns the road to Hesperos, a world whose people never die. The contents promise the shining city of Lucetta, a great cloud-screen that hides the stars, and a law of vanishing by mortal wound. Courts there sentence a culprit to eternal punishment.
70463-the-pennsylvania-journal-of-prison:
A quarterly journal of prison reform dates its third number of volume eight to July 1853. E C and J Biddle published it at Philadelphia. The Philadelphia Society for Alleviating the Miseries of Public Prisons, founded in 1787, directs it. The price is one dollar a year.

Its motto quotes the English inspectors: the separation of one prisoner from another is the only sound basis of reformatory discipline. Articles treat the former times and these, inspectors of prisons, and prison matters at the West. Uncertainty of conviction and punishment gets a hard look. Recent occurrences in Philadelphia fill the news. Short pieces treat indiscriminate almsgiving, the Elizabeth Fry Refuge, and the Ohio Lunatic Asylum. Charles Sumner's praise fronts the number: no American publication held more prison knowledge.
71436-a-narrative-of-travels-on-the-amaz:
A Narrative of Travels on the Amazon and Rio Negro is the travel book of Alfred Wallace, the great student of the wild world. It came out at London in the mid eighteen fifties, with a map and pictures. The shops title for it, a tale of the valley of the great river, sells its scope.

Its first words tell what drove the trip. A keen wish to see a land of heat, says Wallace, and to see with his own eyes the wealth of beast and plant life said to dwell there. Those sights he had read of with joy in the tales of past rovers. So he broke the chains of trade and the ties of home, and set out for a far land of no end summer. The book tells what he found: tribes, clime, rocks, and wild things.
71660-to-make-a-hero:
Randall Garrett wrote To Make a Hero, a science fiction tale printed in Infinity in October 1957. Emsh drew the pictures. The editor's note calls it science fiction told from a historian's viewpoint, setting the record straight on one Leland Hale.

Fraud, larceny, and murder, the teaser says, were all in a day's work to Hale, savior of Cardigan's Green. Garrett opens on the slipperiness of history: men twist the past, he argues, because they think changing it can change the present. The average man prefers romantic legend to fact. Archives of the Interstellar Police, he claims, hold the true tale.
72037-odyssey-of-a-hero:
Odyssey of a Hero, a novel by Vardis Fisher, was published in Philadelphia in 1937. Private John Benton came home from France in 1919 no giant of a hero, but a sound warrior. Three nations had decorated him, and half the women in Paris had kissed him. His Idaho home town gave him a welcome that rocked the state. Seven speeches and a dozen bands marked the day.

Fame went to his head a little, yet Benton remembered that war was dark, blind butchery. German soldiers, hungry for cigarettes and peace, were men like himself. He wants quiet and forgetting, and dreads the fierce joy of stay-at-home patriots who never saw horror in young faces. Fisher traces a hero's hard return to peace.
72084-travels-in-western-africa-in-the-y:
Major William Gray and staff surgeon Dochard wrote Travels in Western Africa in the years 1818 to 1821, printed in London in 1825 with a map, drawings, and costumes. Their route ran from the River Gambia through Woolli, Bondoo, Galam, Kasson, Kaarta, and Foolidoo to the River Niger. Bokari the Kaarta guide fronts the volume in a plate.

Gray gives the book to Earl Bathurst, the colonial secretary, with sentiments of highest respect and sincere gratitude. Though not born in the camp, he was early taught the frankness that characterises the soldier, he says in the preface. He reached Africa remembering the labours of earlier explorers who perished in the search. West African travel readers get the Peddie expedition record.
72159-the-further-adventures-of-zorro:
Johnston McCulley wrote further adventures of Zorro, printed in 1922 after The Mark of Zorro. Land rats and water rats opens the tale, as a sinister vessel, craft of ill omen, sails slowly under spare canvas with lights unburning. She seems to fear reaching her destination too soon, and the hiss of waters round her hull sets the mood.

Pedro the boaster, sudden turmoil, and Fray Felipe making a vow follow. Zorro takes the trail and strikes, walks the plank, and rescues in turn. A dead pirate, a goblet, singing caballeros, and a wild ride fill the mid chapters. The senorita plots also, and Fray Felipe gets his goblet at the close of a swift masked avenger tale in old California.
72170-the-sailor-hero:
Captain F C Armstrong wrote The Sailor Hero, or The Frigate and the Lugger, a sea tale issued at London. Armstrong had written The Cruise of the Daring and The Two Midshipmen. The tale opens as war with France begins.

Lord Hood hoists his flag on the Victory, a ship of one hundred guns, and sails from Spithead. Two midshipmen stand out: William Thornton, the Admiral's favoured lad, and Henry Howard Etherton. Thornton, sixteen or seventeen, is high-spirited and well liked. His birth is a puzzle, since some paid richly for his schooling. Etherton, a baronet's younger son, spreads tales about him. Rivalry drives the tale.
74618-cagliostro:
Trowbridge wrote Cagliostro: The Splendour and Misery of a Master of Magic, printed at New York in nineteen ten. A front list of sources shows how hard the tale is to pin down. French state files hold police notes from the trial of the necklace, which sought to prove Cagliostro was a fraud named Joseph Balsamo. Letters and arrest notes from the seventeen seventies and eighties fill the file.

Trowbridge weighs printed lives, news sheets, and private notes from across Europe. Many of the sources, he warns, are worth little on their own. The book tracks a man who posed as a count, healer, and seer at the courts of Europe. His fall in Rome and Paris ends the tale of fame and ruin.
75566-visibility-zero:
John Amid's story Visibility Zero asks whether an airmail pilot who flies in foul weather is yellow, foolish, or simply human. Bill Melford, senior pilot on the line, refuses a passenger on a night mail run. A twenty mile wind howls outside the cold hangar as reports from Chicago stay poor.

Field manager Feldman holds a form letter from superintendent Hendricks urging help for Webber, a traveller keen to reach Chicago. Company rule leaves passenger decisions to each pilot alone, whatever the load allows. Melford, once branded Wild Bill before safety publicity dropped the word, sets the lead others follow. Pat Grady and Crager, due with a feeder plane, may face the same plea.
76338-el-toro:
El Toro, a motor car story of interior Cuba, is a travel book by Ralph Estep, published at Detroit in 1909. The Packard Motor Car Company issued the book, printed at Buffalo in that year. A frontispiece shows a mountain pass of the route in the island. One wheel ran on a sloping side wall and the other on the crest of the deepest rut there.

The list of illustrations reads like a log of the hardships of the road in Cuba. Everywhere was stone, says another caption, and each mile was gained by defiant effort on the way. The book is a maker record of an early motor tour, part advertisement and part adventure. It shows what motoring meant in 1909 where roads were tracks and a tour was an expedition in itself.
76571-death-of-a-hero:
Richard Aldington published Death of a Hero, a novel, at New York in 1929, reaching a fourth printing by October of that year. A Walpole motto mocks how we trifle away youth before growing old in England. Aldington explains himself in a letter to Halcott Glover instead of a preface.

He and Glover, he says, belong to the generation that spent childhood struggling in the toils of the Victorians and early manhood in the European War. A great number of its men died prematurely. He began the book just after the Armistice in a little Belgian cottage that was his billet. Readers get one of the famous angry novels of the war generation.
78261-a-city-milk-and-cream-contest-as-a:
City Milk and Cream Contest is a government circular on improving the milk supply, issued in 1907. It is circular number 117 of the Bureau of Animal Industry of the Department of Agriculture. Lane, assistant chief of the dairy division, and Weld, assistant dairyman, wrote the circular. The Government Printing Office printed it at Washington, issued 28 October 1907.

 The contest of the title scores the milk and cream of a city by samples in a public competition. Dairymen and dealers are judged on cleanliness and quality before the city in the scheme. Such contests were the dairy division chosen instrument of reform in those years. Rather than prosecute dirty milk, the department shamed and praised it in public, with score cards and prizes. The circular is a small classic of the pure food era, when the milk of great cities was a standing danger to their children.
78916-the-story-of-cairo:
Stanley Lane-Poole, professor of Arabic at Trinity College Dublin, wrote The Story of Cairo for the London house of Dent. The first edition came in 1902, and this hosted copy is the second, from 1906. An old saying stands at the front: he who has not seen Cairo has not seen the world.

The contents move from the living city to its deep past. The first chapter walks the two Cairos, the European and the Egyptian, through shops, homes, and feast days. Then the book steps back to the Arab conquest and the founding of Fustat, the town of the tent. Later chapters treat the suburbs raised by the caliphs' governors. Readers get a city told layer by layer, mosque, gate, and street.
79686-he-would-be-a-hero:
He Would Be a Hero, by Ray Humphreys, author of The Marsh Spook, is a western story set in Monte Vista on rodeo day. Sheriff Joe Cook begs his deputy, Shorty McKay, to skip the covered wagon race and help hunt Manuel Perida, who has shot two men and vanished into the rodeo crowd.

Shorty chooses the race, and the sheriff takes his badge on the spot, calling him a fool in Barnum's phrase. Then Cook phones a dozen trusted young men to raise a posse. Humphreys tells it in thick cowboy speech, with pride and duty pulling one small man in two directions.
8857-the-life-studies-and-works-of-benja:
John Galt composes this 1820 life of Benjamin West, president of the Royal Academy of London, from materials furnished by West himself, and inscribes it to Alexander Gordon. Galt's preface explains that West's professional life formed part of a larger historical work. It could only appear as an episode, and that he once meant to prepare the whole memoirs separately. A careful review of the manuscript, he says, changed his plan into this volume.

Part one follows West from his Pennsylvania Quaker boyhood, through his early painting in America, to London, royal patronage, and the presidency of the Academy. Galt, novelist and friend, writes with firsthand warmth about an artist who painted American history for a British king. The life remains a key source on West and on the art world of Georgian London, best read beside West's paintings themselves.
9847-bacon-is-shake-speare-together-with:
Sir Edwin Durning-Lawrence wrote Bacon Is Shake-Speare in 1910, arguing that Francis Bacon wrote the plays known as Shakespeare's. The book opens by calling the plays the greatest birth of time and their author the greatest genius of all ages. Classical scholars, Durning-Lawrence notes, marvel at the plays' lore, while lawyers rank their author among law's great minds. From such learning, he builds his case for Bacon.

The volume also reprints Bacon's Promus of Formularies and Elegancies, collated from the original manuscript. Plates from Sylva Sylvarum add visual evidence. A reader gets a classic statement of the Baconian heresy, and a window on how fiercely authorship debates once burned.
a-discourse-on-the-life-character-and-wr: William Cullen Bryant delivers a discourse on the life, character, and writings of Gulian Crommelin Verplanck. Spoken before the New York Historical Society on May 17, 1870, it praises Verplanck as scholar and citizen. The society thanked Bryant for an eloquent and instructive address and asked for a copy for publication. The discourse preserves a portrait of a leading New York man of letters.
bacon-is-shake-speare-together-with-a-re:
Sir Edwin Durning-Lawrence published this Baconian argument in 1910, its title stating the whole thesis: Bacon is Shake-Speare. A reprint of Bacon's Promus of Formularies and Elegancies fills the second half, collated with the original manuscript by F. B. Bickley and revised by F. A. Herbert of the British Museum. The plays, he grants, are the greatest birth of time; only a Bacon could have written them.

Pages attack the Stratford man's legend piece by piece. Durning-Lawrence denies that Shakespeare was ever an important actor, a theatre manager, or a company owner. Rowe's tale that his top part was the Ghost in Hamlet is a grotesque fable, accepted for two hundred years without proof. Classical learning and legal knowledge in the plays become his exhibits in a confident, combative brief.
britannica-1911-accolti-pietro:
Pietro Accolti (1455-1532), brother of Bernardo, was known as the cardinal of Ancona. Born at Florence, he became bishop of Ancona in 1505 and cardinal in 1511 under Julius II. Serving as abbreviator, an official who drafts papal documents, under Leo X, he drew up the bull against Luther in 1520. He died at Rome after holding many sees, ending as archbishop of Ravenna.

Confusion with a nephew fills the entry's second half. A younger Benedetto Accolti followed Pietro in several posts, became cardinal in 1527, and wrote in defence of papal claims and as a Latin poet. The entry separates the two men's careers so readers do not merge them.
britannica-1911-achillini-alessandro:
Alessandro Achillini (1463-1512) was an Italian thinker born at Bologna. He lectured in medicine at Bologna and at Padua. He also lectured in philosophy at both schools. Contemporaries styled him a second Aristotle. His works on philosophy were printed at Venice in 1508. They filled one large folio volume. Reprints with large additions followed three times. He died at Bologna in 1512.

Anatomy shared his fame. He wrote a work on the anatomy of the human body. He also wrote a set of anatomical notes. The entry sends readers to the article on anatomy for that work. His brother Giovanni wrote verse and prose. A grand-nephew, Claudio, became a lawyer. Claudio won some note as a versifier.
britannica-1911-alcionio-pietro:
Alcionio, Pietro, or Petrus Alcyonius, an Italian classical scholar who lived from about 1487 to 1527, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Venice, he studied Greek under Marcus Musurus of Candia. For a time he worked for the great printer Aldus Manutius as a corrector of the press. Through Giulio de' Medici he became professor of Greek at Florence in 1522.

When his patron became Pope Clement VII in 1523, Alcionio followed him to Rome and stayed until his death. His Latin translation of Aristotle, published at Venice in 1521, was shown by Sepulveda to be very incorrect. Worse, an enemy accused him of stealing his dialogue on exile from Cicero's lost De Gloria and destroying the only copy. Tiraboschi later showed that charge groundless. Contemporaries still spoke badly of him, the entry adds, calling him haughty, uncouth, vain, and licentious.
britannica-1911-alghero:
Catalonian speech still rings in Alghero, a Sardinian seaport that Aragon ruled for close to four hundred years. The town stands on the island's west coast in Sassari province, twenty-one miles south-south-west of Sassari by rail, and held 10,779 people in 1901. It is a bishop's see set up in 1503, yet its cathedral dates to the twelfth century. Strong walls of medieval times once ringed it.

The Doria house of Genoa founded Alghero near 1102. Aragon seized it in 1354 and beat off attack after attack until, in 1720, it passed to Savoy with the rest of Sardinia. Charles V called there in 1541 on his way to Africa. Coral work and fishing head its trades, with good wine behind them. Close by lie Porto Conte, a harbour safe in all weather, the sea cave of Neptune at Capo Caccia, and an old burial ground dug out in 1904.
britannica-1911-aselli-gasparo: Gasparo Aselli, who lived from 1581 to 1626, was an Italian physician born at Cremona, and his short article follows a botany entry in the hosted text. The 1911 Britannica entry records that he became professor of anatomy and surgery at Pavia and later practised medicine at Milan, where he died. His fame rests on one find, the discovery of the lacteal vessels in the body. That discovery was set out in his work De Lactibus, printed at Milan in 1627, the year after his death.
britannica-1911-aveiro:
Aveiro is a Portuguese seaport and district capital on the river Vouga, built on the south shore of a marshy lagoon dotted with small islands. The town, an episcopal see formerly in Beira province, had 9,979 people in 1900. A canal cut between 1801 and 1808 gives access to the Atlantic.

Salt making, fishing and curing sardines and oysters, and gathering water plants fill local work, with trade in wine, oil, and fruit. Aveiro is probably the Roman Talabriga. In the 16th century its fleet of over sixty ships sailed yearly to the Newfoundland fishing grounds for cod. The district around it, with copper and lead mines and good pasture, held 303,169 people.
britannica-1911-barlow-sir-george-hilaro:
Sir George Hilaro Barlow (1762–1847) was an Anglo-Indian statesman. He joined the Bengal Civil Service in 1778 and in 1788 carried into execution the permanent settlement of Bengal, the great land revenue arrangement. Made a baronet in 1803, he was named provisional governor-general when the marquess of Cornwallis died in 1805.

Barlow's passion for economy in that post won him an odd fame: the only governor-general, the entry says, who diminished the area of British territory. London rejected his appointment all the same, and Lord Minto went out instead. As governor of Madras his want of tact provoked a mutiny of officers in 1809. Recalled in 1812, he lived in retirement until his death in February 1847.
britannica-1911-bembo-pietro:
Pietro Bembo (1470–1547) was an Italian cardinal and scholar born at Venice. A boyhood stay in Florence gave him a lifelong love of Tuscan speech over his own city’s dialect. Two years of Greek study under Lascaris at Messina finished his schooling, and he chose the church.

Bembo served as secretary to Pope Leo X, then lived at Padua in literary ease before Venice made him its historian and librarian of St Mark’s. Paul III gave him a cardinal’s hat in 1539, with the sees of Gubbio and Bergamo after. As a writer he was the great purist of his age, holding exact copying of classic style the highest aim.
britannica-1911-bertinoro:
Bertinoro is a town and episcopal see in Emilia, Italy, in the province of Forli. It stands 800 feet above sea level on Apennine foothills. The 1911 Britannica entry gives 3,753 people in the town in 1901, and 7,786 in the commune. From the town the view runs north over the Emilia plain. The lower course of the Po lies within that view.

The town seems first fortified by Frederick Barbarossa. Its castle stood many sieges in the middle ages. The castle is now almost wholly ruined. The church of S. Donato survives, a Lombard work with Byzantine capitals. Nearby Polenta was the birthplace of Francesca da Rimini. The poet Carducci wrote a fine ode on its church, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-bonghi-ruggero:
Ruggero Bonghi (1828–1895) was an Italian scholar and politician famed for a biting tongue in print and in parliament. Born at Naples, he was exiled after the rising of 1848, fled Tuscany for an article against the Bourbons, and settled at Turin. There he went back to philosophy and to translating Plato.

He refused a Greek chair at Pavia under Austria in 1858 and took it from the Italian government in 1859. Elected a deputy in 1860, he backed Cavour's party and the historic Right, and in 1870 he defended the law of guarantees for the Lanza cabinet. Yet his wit spared no one, friend or foe. He also edited the Milan paper Perseveranza and held a Latin chair at Florence.
britannica-1911-calderon-de-la-barca-ped:
Pedro Calderón de la Barca (1600–1681) was a Spanish dramatist and poet. This long 1911 Britannica biography gives his life and work. He was born at Madrid on 17 January 1600. His mother died in 1610, and his father in 1615. He studied at the Jesuit College in Madrid. He then read law at Salamanca. He won prizes at literary contests held for St Isidore.

A violent episode marks his early fame. In 1629 an actor stabbed his brother Diego. The man took sanctuary in a convent. Calderón and his friends broke into the cloister after him. A famous preacher denounced the act before Philip IV. Calderón answered with a mocking line in a play. He was briefly jailed for the insult. When Lope de Vega died in 1635, Calderón stood first among Spanish dramatists. His brother José edited a volume of his plays in 1636. The article follows his long court career from there.
britannica-1911-capponi-piero:
Piero Capponi (1447–1496) was a Florentine statesman and warrior. This 1911 Britannica entry tells of his stand against France. He was meant for a business career at first. Lorenzo de' Medici saw his ability, though. Lorenzo sent him as ambassador to several courts. He served there with distinction for years. When Lorenzo died in 1492, his weak son Piero succeeded. Capponi led the faction that opposed the Medici.

In 1494 that faction expelled the Medici from Florence. Capponi became chief of the restored republic. That year Charles VIII of France invaded Italy. The exiled Medici sheltered in the French camp. Charles entered Florence with his army in November. He behaved like the city's conqueror from the first day. The citizens armed, and street fighting began to break out. Charles then lowered his tone about the Medici. Money terms caused fresh quarrels between the two sides.
britannica-1911-catanzaro:
Catanzaro is a town and bishop seat of Calabria, Italy, on high ground. Its town entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the capital of Catanzaro province, over a thousand feet up. Counts from nineteen o one put the town at near twenty three thousand people.

The town enjoys a cool summer climate and commands fine wide views. Many wealthy families make their homes in the town all year. Trade in olive oil, silk, and velvet forms its chief business base. A castle built by Robert Guiscard has been much modernized since then. The see was founded in eleven twenty one, and a museum holds old coins.
britannica-1911-cattaro:
Cattaro is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the chief town of a district in Dalmatia, then part of Austria. In its own tongue it is Kotor. The count of 1900 gave 3,021 people in the town and 5,418 in the commune. It sits on a narrow ledge between high hills and the sea.

Below it lies the Bocche di Cattaro, a winding inlet of the Adriatic that spreads into five broad gulfs. Those gulfs form one of the finest natural harbours in Europe. The town is strongly fortified, with some three thousand troops near by. Castelnuovo guards the main entrance on the sea side. On land, long walls climb from the town to the castle of San Giovanni high above.
britannica-1911-cavallini-pietro:
Pietro Cavallini (c. 1259–1344) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an Italian painter born in Rome, of the earliest epoch of the modern Roman school. Giotto taught him painting and mosaic while working at Rome. He is believed to have helped his master on the Navicella mosaic of St Peter. He also studied under the Cosmati. Lanzi praised his skill in both painting and mosaic.

His grand fresco of a Crucifixion at Assisi survives in fair condition. He was versed in architecture and sculpture as well. One claim links him to the mosaics of Edward the Confessor's tomb in Westminster Abbey in 1279. The entry notes that a comparison of dates undermines that claim. He died in 1344 at the age of eighty five, famed for piety. Important works by him in Santa Cecilia in Trastevere had lately been found when the entry was written.
britannica-1911-colletta-pietro:
Pietro Colletta is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in 1775, he was a general and historian of Naples. He joined the Neapolitan gun arm in 1796 and fought the French in 1798.

The article follows a career tossed by war and revolt. When the French set up a short lived republic at Naples, he stood with it. On the king's return he was jailed and barely escaped death by the use of bribes. Restored to rank in 1806, he rose to general in 1812. He fought the Austrians in 1815 and kept his rank when the old king came back. In the revolt of 1820 he crushed a rising in Sicily with a hard hand. Exiled in the end, he spent his last years at Florence on a history of Naples.
britannica-1911-coro:
Coro, a small city in Venezuela, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the capital of the state of Falcon, seven miles west of its port, La Vela de Coro. A rail line links the two, and Caracas lies 199 miles away. The entry gives it about 9,500 people in 1904.

Coro stands on a sandy plain between the Caribbean and the Gulf of Venezuela. Its height above the sea is only 105 feet, and its climate is hot but not unhealthy. The city is badly built, with unpaved streets and few fine public buildings save two old churches. It trades for a wide district east of Lake Maracaibo. Its exports include goat skins, fine tobacco, coffee, cacao, and dyewoods. Coro was founded in 1527 and was made a bishopric in 1536.
britannica-1911-covilham-pero:
Pero de Covilham (flourished 1487–1525) was a Portuguese explorer and diplomat, a native of Covilhã in Beira. In early life he went to Castile and served a duke of Seville. When war broke out between Castile and Portugal, he came home. He joined the court of King Alphonso V, first as groom and then as squire. John II kept him in that service.

On 7 May 1487 the king sent him east with Alphonso de Payva. Their mission was to search the Levant and the lands of Asia and Africa near it. They were also to find the land of Prester John by overland routes. At that same hour Bartholomeu Diaz sailed to seek the end of Africa by sea. The two men carried a letter of credence for all lands and a map of the world.
britannica-1911-damiani-pietro:
Pietro Damiani (about 1007–1072) was one of the most famed churchmen of the 1000s, born at Ravenna after a youth of hardship. He won a name as a teacher, then left the world about 1035 for the hermitage of Fonte Avellana. By 1043 he headed that house. He set a harsher discipline there, flagellation included, and the house became a model for others. His Liber Gomorrhianus of 1049 denounced the vices of the clergy to Pope Leo IX.

Damiani worked with Hildebrand in the reform of the church and counselled a line of popes. Made cardinal bishop of Ostia against his own wish, he defended Rome's authority at Milan in 1059. He served as legate to France, Florence, and Germany, where in 1069 he turned Henry IV from divorcing his wife. His fiercest wrath fell on simony and on married clergy. He died at Faenza on 22 February 1072, leaving letters, sermons, and an office of the Virgin.
britannica-1911-entre-minho-e-douro:
Entre Minho e Douro, popularly called Minho, is a former province of northern Portugal. It is bounded north by Galicia in Spain, east by Traz-os-Montes, south by Beira, and west by the Atlantic Ocean. Its population in 1900 was 1,170,361, and its area 2790 square miles. The coast is level, broken only by river mouths.

Inland the ground rises toward the north and east, where ranges such as the Serra da Peneda at 4728 feet mark the frontier. As its name says, the province is bounded by two great rivers, the Douro on the south and the Minho on the north. The climate is mild, and palms and aloes grow in the open all year. Wheat, maize, wine, olives, and chestnuts are the chief products. The entry stresses the dense, hard-working peasantry, farming closely with primitive tools, and names Oporto, Braga, and Guimarães among its towns.
britannica-1911-espartero-baldomero:
Baldomero Espartero, who lived from 1792 to 1879, was a Spanish soldier and statesman with a string of high titles. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born on the twenty-seventh of February 1792. He was the ninth child of a carter who wished to make him a priest. At fifteen the boy enlisted to fight the armies of Napoleon. In 1811 he became a lieutenant of engineers at Cadiz.

Espartero then crossed to America in 1815 to fight the colonies in revolt. For eight years he won rank on the field, and was cut down at last with Spain's loss at Ayacucho. Back in Spain he settled at Logroño and wed a rich heiress. When the Carlist War broke out, he backed the young queen Isabella. He beat the Carlists in clash after clash and rose fast to high command.
britannica-1911-fernandez-alvaro:
Alvaro Fernandez, one of the leading Portuguese explorers of the early fifteenth century, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was raised in the household of Prince Henry, called the Navigator. Still young and bold, he took a large part in the finding of the Guinea coast. He was a nephew of the man who had found the Madeira islands again in Henry's service.

The article says that when the great expedition of 1445 sailed for West Africa, his uncle gave him a fine caravel. He was told above all to push discovery, the aim his prince held most dear. Fernandez outran all the prince's other servants as a pioneer at that time. He passed the mouth of the Senegal, rounded Cape Verde, and reached the Cape of Masts. The next year he sailed on much farther down the coast.
britannica-1911-fontana-prospero:
Prospero Fontana (1512-1597), Italian painter, was born in Bologna and became a pupil of Innocenzo da Imola. He afterwards worked for Vasari and for Perino del Vaga. From Vasari, probably, he took a habit of showy, offhand work. He took on a multitude of commissions and painted fast. He is said to have covered a whole hall in the Vitelli palace in a few weeks. Speed, daring and fertility of invention mark all his work, the entry shows.

Alongside those gifts, the entry faults Fontana's incorrect drawing and mannerism. He belongs to the declining Bolognese school. His soundest successes came in portraiture. About 1550 Michelangelo presented him to Pope Julius III as a portrait-painter, and the pope pensioned him. He is also remembered as the father of Lavinia Fontana.
britannica-1911-fuero:
Fuero is a Spanish term from the Latin forum, meaning a right, privilege, or charter. The entry traces it to the Roman assize districts of Spain, where magistrates deferred to the standing local custom of each place. Gothic and even Arab rule seem to have left much of that municipal order in place, and when the word appears in 10th-century documents the thing it names is already old.

The earliest surviving written fuero is that granted to Leon by Alphonso V in 1020, part general statutes and part town charter. Jaca in 1064 and Logroño in 1095 set patterns copied widely, and Toledo charter of 1101, enlarged in 1118, grounded many Castilian fueros. In time the word widened to mean a general code of laws. The closing history follows the Basque fueros: set aside after 1833 amid civil war, acknowledged again in 1839, and finally extinguished in 1876 after the Carlist rising.
britannica-1911-gabbro:
Gabbro, in petrology, names a group of coarse, deep-seated basic rocks made essentially of a basic plagioclase felspar with one or more dark iron-magnesia minerals. Augite, hornblende, hypersthene and olivine are the common partners of the felspar, which is mostly labradorite or bytownite. The gabbros match the dolerites, basalts and diabases in mineral content but differ in structure, standing as their deep-seated equivalents. Their felspars often alter into cloudy masses of saussurite, a tough greenish-white material without cleavage.

Many gabbro minerals hold tiny dark enclosures ranged along crystal planes, and light reflected from them gives the shimmer called schiller. Chemically the gabbros are low in silica and rich in iron, magnesia and lime, which sets them apart from granites and peridotites. They serve as building stones, and iron-ore segregations found with them in Norway and Sweden are sometimes mined.
britannica-1911-gavazzi-alessandro:
Alessandro Gavazzi (1809-1889) was an Italian preacher and patriot, born at Bologna on 21 March 1809. The 1911 Britannica entry makes him a Barnabite monk from 1825, teaching rhetoric at Naples, then called to Rome in 1840 after speaking liberal views. When the French took Rome he left Italy.

From exile he campaigned against priests and Jesuits across England, Scotland and North America, partly through his paper, the Gavazzi Free Word. In 1855 he joined the Evangelical church and organized Italian Protestants in London. Back in Italy in 1860 he served as chaplain with Garibaldi. In 1870 he headed the Free Church of Italy, united its congregations, and in 1875 founded its theological college at Rome, where he taught. He died at Rome on 9 January 1889.
britannica-1911-giannone-pietro:
Pietro Giannone is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Ischitella on the seventh of May 1676, he was an Italian writer on law and the past. He came to Naples at the age of eighteen to read law.

The article centres on his great work, printed in 1723. It tells the civil history of the kingdom of Naples over twenty years of labour. In it he took the side of the state against the church of Rome. He was the first, the text says, to treat that clash in a set order. The church struck back hard. His book was banned, and he was cast out of the church. Driven from Naples, he found shelter and a pension at Vienna. Later years brought fresh exile and a cell at Turin.
britannica-1911-goldsboro:
Goldsboro, a city in North Carolina, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It is the county-seat of Wayne county. It stands on the Neuse river, south-east of Raleigh. Three rail lines serve it. Its people grew from about four thousand in 1890 to just over six thousand in 1910.

The land around it yields large crops of tobacco, cotton, and grain. Truck farming is a big trade there. The city is a shipping point for strawberries and many kinds of vegetables. Its factories make cotton goods, knit goods, and cotton-seed oil. Farm tools, lumber, and furniture are also made there. The city is the seat of a state asylum and of an Odd Fellows' orphan home. The town runs its own water works. The piece gives a full civic sketch of a small Southern city of the day.
britannica-1911-gondokoro:
Gondokoro is a government station and trading place on the east bank of the upper Nile. It is the head station of the Northern Province of the British Uganda protectorate. It lies 1,070 miles by river south of Khartum. The station stands on a cliff twenty-five feet above the river and is held to be very unhealthy.

Huts of the Bari people stand near the houses of the civil and army staff. The weight of Gondokoro lies in its place on the river. It stands a few miles from the top limit of boat travel up the Nile from Khartum. From there the road to Uganda goes on by land. Europeans first reached it in 1841-1842. It soon grew into a hub of the ivory and slave trades.
britannica-1911-grant-george-monro:
George Monro Grant was head of Queen University at Kingston in Ontario. He lived from eighteen thirty five to nineteen o two. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Nova Scotia, he studied at Glasgow university with high honours.

Grant joined the Presbyterian ministry and held a Halifax charge for years. His preaching and his speeches on public themes won him wide fame. When Canada joined as one in eighteen sixty seven, he backed the union. Nova Scotia had fought that union most, yet his voice helped it win. He crossed the land with rail survey crews and wrote Ocean to Ocean.
britannica-1911-hero:
Heroes of Greek cult are weighed in a study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. A hero was a warrior of rare strength and nerve, the entry says. The word also fits all who stand above their fellows in worth. No sure root for the Greek word has yet been found. In old Greece such heroes drew a cult of their own.

That cult bound them deep into the land's rite life. Some hold the heroes were real men raised by fame. Some hold they were signs of the forces of nature. The more held view makes them gods sunk to a lower rank. Rohde's view makes them souls of the dead raised high. The cult, at root, was worship of honoured ancestors.
britannica-1911-hunter-robert-mercer-tal:
Robert Mercer Taliaferro Hunter, who lived from 1809 to 1887, was an American statesman from Virginia. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him from the university of Virginia to the bar in 1830. State and national house seats filled the next decade of his public life. He served as Speaker of the national house from 1839 to 1841.

From 1847 to 1861 he sat in the senate and led its finance committee. Credit is given him for cutting the silver in small coins of the realm. He wrote the Tariff Act of 1857 and the bonded warehouse system as well. In 1853 he declined an offer to become secretary of state.
britannica-1911-jaro:
Jaro, a town in the province of Iloílo on Panay in the Philippine Islands, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Jaro river, two miles north west of the town of Iloílo, the capital. The count in 1903 was 10681 people. The town lies on a plain in the midst of a rich farm district.

Fine houses mark the town, along with a cathedral church. A curious tower of three tiers draws the eye as well. A paper comes out twice a week, and a second one each month. Spanish settlers founded Jaro in 1584. From 1903 until February 1908 it formed part of the town of Iloílo. Then it stood apart once more as its own town.
britannica-1911-la-marmora-alfonso-ferre:
Alfonso Ferrero La Marmora (1804–1878) was an Italian general and statesman, born at Turin on the 18th of November 1804. He joined the Sardinian army in 1823 and rose to major at the siege of Peschiera in 1848. That August he freed King Charles Albert from the Milan revolutionaries, and in October became general and minister of war. He held the war office, with one break for the Crimean command, until 1859. He rebuilt the Piedmontese army and fought in the war of 1859 against Austria.

In July 1859 La Marmora followed Cavour as premier. As premier from September 1864 he claimed for Italy full freedom over Rome in a note on the September Convention. In April 1866 he made the alliance with Prussia against Austria, and in June led an army corps in the war. He was beaten at Custozza on the 23rd of June and was accused of treason and of double dealing by the Prussians.
britannica-1911-leoncavallo-ruggiero: Ruggiero Leoncavallo (born 1858) was an Italian opera composer born at Naples. Training at the conservatoire there came first. Years of teaching and failed stage bids followed. Pagliacci won at once at Milan in 1892. His Medici and Chatterton found no favour. La Bohème at Venice in 1897 gave firm backing. Zaza came in 1900 and Der Roland in 1904. He wrote his own words for each opera.
britannica-1911-lillibullero:
Lillibullero is the name of a song that swept England late in the 1600s. Soldiers and backers of William III sang it most. The Irish war of the Revolution of 1688 gave it its hour. The tune was far older than the words. An Irish nurse's song had used it early in the century.

Crude verses, most often laid to Thomas Wharton, mocked Talbot, earl of Tyrconnel. James had made Talbot his deputy in Ireland in 1687. The song's refrain gave the piece its name. Macaulay tells how all classes sang the rhyme from end to end of England. Wharton boasted he had sung a king out of three kingdoms. The cooler view here is that the song rode a mood. It did not make that mood.
britannica-1911-mascagni-pietro:
Pietro Mascagni, an Italian opera composer born in 1863, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Leghorn, the son of a baker, he was schooled for the law. He let his law studies slide for music and took secret lessons at a local institute. A symphony of his was played in 1879, and a rich amateur paid for his study at the Milan Conservatoire.

He soon left Milan to conduct a touring opera company. After lean years he leapt to fame at Rome in 1890 with his one act opera Cavalleria Rusticana, whose intermezzo was played everywhere. The entry then tracks a long slide: L'Amico Fritz, Iris, and more operas were met coldly. He ran the Pesaro Conservatoire from 1895 to 1903, then lost the post after a tour of the United States.
britannica-1911-middleboro:
Middleboro, a township in Plymouth county, Massachusetts, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It lies in the south east of the state, bounded by the Taunton river. Its population rose from 6,065 in 1890 to 8,214 in the census of 1910. The township covers about seventy square miles.

The main village shares the township's name and lies thirty five miles south of Boston. Rail and electric lines link it with Taunton, Boston, and other towns. The village has a town house, a soldiers' monument, and a public library. A merchant of the town left a large fund for its benefit. Income from that fund has built roads, raised an almshouse, and added special courses at the high school. The village is also a summer resort.
britannica-1911-montoro: Montoro is a town of southern Spain, in the province of Cordova, covered in a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands twenty-seven miles east of the city of Cordova, on the Madrid to Cordova railway, with 14,581 people in 1900. The town was the Epora of the Romans and became a strong Moorish fortress in the middle ages, though largely rebuilt since. It sits on a rocky peninsula on the south bank of the Guadalquivir, crossed by a fine four-arched bridge from the sixteenth century.
britannica-1911-paez-pedro:
Pedro Paez, who lived from 1564 to 1622, was a Jesuit envoy to Abyssinia. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica recounts his hard road there. He was born at Olmedo in Old Castile. He joined the Society of Jesus and was sent to Goa in 1588.

Pirates seized Paez on his first trip and held him as a slave in Yemen. Freed after seven years, he worked in India, then reached Abyssinia in 1603. He learned the chief tongues, taught children, and preached at court. His teaching helped turn the ruler toward Rome, a step that sparked civil war. Paez is said to be the first European to see the source of the Blue Nile. He died of fever in 1622.
britannica-1911-perugino-pietro:
Pietro Perugino, born Pietro Vannucci in 1446 at Città della Pieve in Umbria, is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He took his common name from Perugia, the main city near his home. The text notes that his family was well thought of but poor. As a boy under nine he was placed with a painter at Perugia.

Later pages trace his move to Arezzo and then to Florence. There he studied in the shop of Andrea del Verrocchio, where Leonardo was also a pupil. He may have learned his strong skill with depth and space from Piero della Francesca. Readers get a clear path from a poor start to high standing in Italian art.
britannica-1911-pesaro:
Pesaro, a city and seaport of the Marches in Italy, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the capital of its province and stands on the Adriatic coast, 37 miles north-west of Ancona by rail. It lies on the right bank of the river Foglia. The ground of the city is low, only ten to forty feet above the sea, but hills ring it on both sides.

The article points to a hill villa of fame. Its first stone was laid by an emperor, it was built by the Sforza family, and its rooms hold fine plaster ceilings, wall paintings, and floors of painted tiles. A new palace was begun in 1530 for Eleonora Gonzaga but never finished. The city walls were turned into a public walk in 1830. The old cathedral holds a floor of mosaic work from the twelfth century.
britannica-1911-pinsuti-ciro: Ciro Pinsuti, an Anglo Italian composer, was born at Siena in eighteen twenty nine. He was trained in music for a career as a pianist, partly in London and partly at Bologna, where he was a pupil of Rossini. From eighteen forty eight he made his home in England and became a teacher of singing. In eighteen fifty six he was made a professor at the Academy of Music in London. He won fame for his favourite songs and part songs.
britannica-1911-stradella-alessandro:
Alessandro Stradella, an Italian composer who lived from about 1645 to 1682, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He ranks among the most accomplished musicians of the seventeenth century. The long told story of his life comes from a French history of music from 1715. That tale mixes his operas with romance and murder.

By the tale, a Venetian noble hired Stradella to teach his mistress to sing. Stradella eloped with her to Rome, and hired killers were sent after them. At a church concert the killers heard his new oratorio and lost heart at its beauty. They warned him instead, and he fled to Turin. There a second band left him for dead on the walls. He lived, wed the lady, and moved to Genoa. A year later a third band killed them both at home. New research, the entry adds, gives a plainer birth and family.
britannica-1911-tagliacozzi-gasparo:
Gasparo Tagliacozzi, who lived from 1546 to 1599, was an Italian surgeon. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica calls him a wonder worker of his day. He was born at Bologna and studied at its university. He took his degree in philosophy and medicine at twenty-four.

Tagliacozzi became a professor of surgery, then of anatomy. His great book came out at Venice in 1597. Its Latin title speaks of surgery for the maimed by grafting. A second title spells out the repair of noses, ears, and lips. The method joined skin taken from the arm to the hurt part. That graft art was unknown to all before him, the title claims. He died at Bologna in 1599.
britannica-1911-toro:
Toro is a town of Spain, in the province of Zamora, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes its old streets and churches. It stands on the right bank of the river Duero, on the Zamora to Medina del Campo railway, with 8,379 people in 1900. A fine bridge of twenty-two arches spans the river.

The entry calls Toro an ancient fortified town with narrow streets, many medieval churches, convents, and palaces. Its cathedral is Romanesque, dating from the twelfth century. A palace in the town hosted the Cortes of 1371, 1442, and 1505, which made Toro and its law code famous. The town played a large part in the growth of Leon and Castile.
britannica-1911-torrigiano-pietro:
Pietro Torrigiano is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Torrigiano was a Florentine sculptor who lived from 1472 to 1522. He studied art in Florence under the patronage of Lorenzo the Magnificent. A tale told by Cellini says he broke the nose of the young Michelangelo with a blow in a quarrel. That mark stayed visible in all later portraits of Michelangelo.

The article follows his work in Rome on stucco decoration for the pope. After time as a hired soldier he was called to England. There he made the grand tomb for King Henry the Seventh and his queen. That tomb still stands in Westminster Abbey and was finished in 1517. Its two figures are praised as well modelled and lifelike. He also made an altar and canopy for the same chapel, later destroyed by Puritans.
britannica-1911-tull-jethro:
Jethro Tull (1674–1741) was an English writer on farming and a farmer. He was born at Basildon in Berkshire in 1674. He entered St John's College, Oxford, in 1691 and was called to the bar in 1699, but he never worked as a lawyer. That year he wed and began to farm his father's land at Howberry, near Wallingford. There, about 1701, he made and honed his drill machine. He began tests of sowing in rows set wide apart.

Wide rows let the plough and hoe work the land through most of the time of growth. In 1709 Tull moved to a farm near Hungerford. From 1711 to 1714 he went through France and Italy, and he watched the farm ways of those lands with care. What he saw backed his thoughts on manure and on the worth of breaking the soil fine.
britannica-1911-vivero:
Vivero, a town in the north west of Spain, is the subject of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in the province of Lugo, on the Ria de Vivero. That inlet is formed by the river Landrove, where it flows into the Bay of Biscay. The entry gives the town a count of 12,843 people in 1900.

Inside, the town is shown as old and scenic, set across the water from the far bank. A bridge of twelve arches and a long causeway link the two sides. Its work rests on a fishing fleet, trade by coast, and farm goods from the rich land around it. The one road inland runs to Cabreiros, for Lugo and Ferrol.
britannica-1911-waynesboro:
Waynesboro is a borough of Franklin county, Pennsylvania, near Antietam Creek, as this 1911 Britannica article describes it. It lies at the foot of South Mountain, with many caves and caverns under the borough. Its people grew from 3,811 in 1890 to 7,199 in 1910, and two railways served it.

A settlement was made on the site about 1734. The place was called Mount Vernon for twenty years, then Wallacetown for an early settler. At the close of the War of Independence it was renamed in honour of General Anthony Wayne. A village was laid out in 1797. Its borough charter, granted in 1818, was repealed in 1824 and revived in 1830, when the spelling was settled as Waynesboro.
captain-jinks-hero:
Ernest Crosby wrote a mock tale of a soldier hero, printed in 1902. Dan Beard drew the plates and the jest cuts. Funk and Wagnalls put out the book at New York and London. Twelve chapters line the frame. A bombshell opens the tale, in jest or in war.

East Point, the cadet school in all but name, comes next. Love and fight share the third. War and trade share the fourth. Slowburgh gives the home town. Off for the Cubapines — Cuba and the Philippines in one jest word — starts the war. San Diego fight, Morito folk, and post at Havilla fill the heart. A great deed of arms, a Gin-Sin meal, and a great white temple close the list in view. Sam, the hero, sits astride a chair in one plate, a mark of the book's soft scorn for war fame.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alfonso-capec:
Alfonso Capecelatro was a cardinal, Archbishop of Capua, and writer, born at Marseilles in February 1824 and dead in November 1912. He descended from the dukes of Castel Pagano. His father, a Napoleonic officer under Murat, fled to Malta and Marseilles when Ferdinand of Naples repressed political liberalism. The family went back to Italy in 1826 and Naples in 1830. Capecelatro gave himself to ecclesiastical studies, especially ecclesiastical history, and to charitable enterprises.

He was drawn to St. Peter Damian, St. Catherine of Siena, St. Philip Neri, and St. Alphonsus Liguori, figures of Italian revival, whose biographies he wrote. He answered Renan's Life of Christ and published his own Life of Jesus Christ, gathering modern research on Hebrew topography and customs, without polemics. He also wrote three volumes on Catholic doctrine, two on the Christian virtues, and sermons. Leo XIII made him assistant librarian at Rome, Archbishop of Capua in 1880, and cardinal in 1885.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alghero:
Alghero is an Italian diocese of twenty-two communes in Sassari province and four in that of Cagliari, in the Archdiocese of Sassari. Genoa's Doria family built the city in 1102, and in 1106 John, Bishop of Alghero, attended the Trinity Church consecration at Sacargia. After a long period of decadence Julius II renewed and confirmed the see by his Bull of 1503.

The Genoese Pietro Parens took the bishopric and sat at the Lateran Council of 1512 from its first through its seventh session. The diocese holds 20 parishes, 71 secular priests, and 54,300 inhabitants today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alphonsus-de-:
Alphonsus de Castro, Friar Minor, born at Zamora in 1495, died at Brussels in 1558. At fifteen he entered a Franciscan convent near Salamanca. He taught theology at Salamanca, serving forty-three years as confessor to Charles V and Philip II and preacher at Spain's court. In 1545 he accompanied Cardinal Grennis to Trent, prominent in the fourth session on Scripture.

As the cardinal's representative he subscribed to its canons. He proposed adding to the Decree on Canonical Scriptures that besides sacred books much else must be held, unwritten, by Church authority. In later sessions he addressed vernacular Scripture and original sin. He accompanied Philip II to England, returning with him in 1557. Appointed to Compostella after Cardinal John Tolenton's death, he died before taking office. Best-known works: Against All Heresies (Cologne 1539) and On the Just Punishment of Heretics (Salamanca 1547). Both appeared in one Paris edition (1571-78).
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-apari:
Antonio Aparisi, a Spanish lawyer and speaker born in Valencia in 1815 and dead in Madrid in 1872, stands at the centre of this Catholic Encyclopedia life story. Trained for the bar in 1839, he won most of his criminal cases and wrote poems and pieces for Catholic papers in Valencia and Madrid. As a deputy for Valencia in the Cortes, the Spanish parliament, he led the royalist group. He spoke for Catholic unity and the pope's temporal power, meaning the pope's rule over land in Italy.

Later work took him to Paris and London on dynastic business, and to a Carlist meeting in Switzerland in 1870. He also wrote treatises with titles such as El Papa y Napoleón and La cuestión dinástica, and he was elected a senator from Guipuzcoa in 1871. His collected works came out in five volumes after his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-barbastro:
Barbastro is a suffragan diocese in Spain, its city standing where the Cinca and Vero rivers meet. Roman Hither Spain once held it, and Arabs under Muza took it in 711, giving the name Barbaschter, source of Barbastrum. Saracens held it until about 1063, when Sancho Ramirez of Aragon retook it. After further Arab seizures, Pedro I restored it to Spain in 1101 and, with papal consent, moved the see there from Roda.

Its first bishop, Poncio, went to Rome to secure permission for the transfer. The diocese, bounded by the Pyrenees, Lérida, Huesca, and Yaca, holds 154 parishes under ten archpriests. About 240,000 people live there, served by some 220 clergy in 231 churches and 177 chapels. King Ramiro the Monk abdicated there in 1134, and its cathedral, palace, seminary, and Piarist college rank among its noted buildings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartolome-de-:
Bartolomé de Torres Naharro was a Spanish poet and dramatist born at Torres, near Badajoz, toward the end of the fifteenth century. A cleric of some learning, he lived at Rome about 1514 as chaplain to his patron Fabricio Colonna. A satire attacking the Court's vices got him banished from Rome, and he took refuge at Naples. There in 1517 appeared his Propaladia, collecting lyrics, satires, epistles, romances, ballads, and eight plays he called Comedias.

Beyond literary merit, the plays matter for his dramatic theory, a model later authors followed. He split comedies into Noticia, from real seen happenings, and Fantasía, from imaginary incidents seeming true. He kept Horace's five acts, renamed Jornadas as mere resting places, and required six to twelve characters. Some plays tend toward the unities of time, place, and action, and his best-known comedies are Himenea, Serafina, and Tinelaria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benito-jeroni:
Benito Jerónimo Feijóo y Montenegro, a celebrated Spanish Benedictine writer, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Galicia in 1676, he died at Oviedo in 1764 after taking the Benedictine habit at San Juan de Samos in 1688. His learning ranged across nearly every branch of knowledge of his day.

Feijóo attacked old customs, superstitions, and stale institutions, and pressed for reform of public teaching in Spain. His essays made him a voice of the Spanish Enlightenment, though he wrote as a monk. The entry presents a critic who used wide reading to clear away error, and who paid for candour with controversy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bertinoro:
Bertinoro, a small city in Romagna, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Anciently Forum Truentinorum, and Petra Honorii in the Gothic war, it takes its present name from that second title. Legend says St. Illuminata of Ravenna fled there about 303 but still met martyrdom.

Until 1360 Bertinoro obeyed the Bishop of Forlimpopoli, but when Cardinal Albornoz destroyed that city, the bishop's seat moved to Bertinoro. The entry first sketches Forlimpopoli, founded in 173 BC, then follows Bertinoro's bishops and churches. It is a compact diocesan history built on a transfer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-borgo-san-sep:
Borgo San-Sepolcro, a diocese in Arezzo province, Tuscany, grew around a tenth-century oratory built by two pilgrims home from Palestine. They set relics from the holy places there, pilgrims flocked in, and a town rose around the shrine, later ruled in time by the abbot of a Camaldoli monastery. Guido Petramala, Bishop of Arezzo, walled it and made it a Ghibelline stronghold.

Subject first to Castello, it became a see under Leo X in 1515, with Giovanni Galeotto Graziani as first bishop. Later bishops include the theologians Nicolo Tornabuoni and Dionisio Bussotti and Gian Lorenzo Tilli, founder of the seminary. Its cathedral, a three-nave Romanesque church leaning toward Gothic, holds the famed Volto Santo, a great wooden crucifix in a long tunic, kept there since the tenth century. The diocese counts 60,500 Catholics and 250 churches and chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catanzaro:
Catanzaro is the capital of Calabria and the seat of a diocese suffragan to Reggio. The date its see was erected is uncertain, but it may go back to 1122, when Pope Callistus II moved the see of Taverna to Catanzaro. The diocese then counted 85,000 people, with 48 parishes and 97 churches and chapels.

Its clergy numbered 116 secular and 4 regular priests, and it held one religious house of men and five of women. The whole entry is a compact statistical portrait of the diocese, giving its size, its parishes, and its clergy without a longer historical narrative.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cattaro:
Cattaro is the chief town of one of Dalmatia's four divisions. It is set beneath steep limestone cliffs on a small Adriatic bay, nearly ringed by mountains. Its gulf, the Bocche di Cattaro, counts among Europe's most picturesque sites. The ancients called the town Ascrivium, and it became a Roman colony early in the Christian era before Saracens destroyed it around 860.

Refugees driven from home by the Hungarians rebuilt it. Cattaro was a republic by the twelfth century. It passed under Byzantine and Serbian rule, allied with King Louis of Hungary in 1368, and submitted to Venice in 1423 while keeping some autonomy. The diocese, suffragan to Zara, counted 13,363 Catholics and 15,000 non-Catholics, with 19 parishes and bishops recorded back to 877.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diego-de-alma:
Diego de Almagro the Elder was, by common report, a foundling. He reached Panama in 1514 and joined Pizarro in the venture that would conquer Peru. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry recounts the partnership of 1524, sealed by a written pact two years later. Both men signed with their marks, since neither could write his name.

Almagro lost an eye to an arrow in a coastal landing. He sailed south for first news of Peru and twice turned back to Panama for stores and men. In doing so he saved Pizarro and his followers from ruin. The entry carries the story through the conquest and the bitter quarrels that followed, pointing readers to the chronicles of Almagro and his son.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elena-lucrezi:
Elena Lucrezia Piscopia Cornaro was a learned Venetian noblewoman, born in 1646 and dead at Padua in 1684. Daughter of Giovanni Battista Cornaro, Procurator of Saint Mark's, she began Latin and Greek at seven and soon mastered them. She went on to Hebrew, Spanish, French, and Arabic, earning the title Oracle of Seven Tongues, and she also studied mathematics, philosophy, and theology.

In 1665 she took the habit of a Benedictine oblate without becoming a nun. At her father's wish she entered Padua University and took a doctorate in philosophy in the cathedral on 25 June 1678, before a crowd of scholars and nobles. A member of several academies and honoured across Europe, she spent her last seven years in study and charity. Her writings, printed at Parma in 1688, mix discourses, translations, and devotional pieces.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fernan-caball:
Fernan Caballero was the pen name of the Spanish novelist Cecilia Bohl von Faber. Born in Switzerland in 1796, she reached Spain with her parents in 1813. Thrice married and widowed, she retired to Seville's royal palace after 1863. Her first novel, La Gaviota, appeared in serial form in 1849.

La Gaviota, The Sea Gull in English, won readers across Europe and beyond. Her novels pictured Andalusian types and customs with charm, grace, and exactness. Critics compared her descriptive power to those of Scott and Cooper. Her complete works filled thirteen volumes published at Madrid.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-lop:
Francisco Lopez-Caro, born at Seville in 1598 and dead at Madrid in 1662, was a Spanish portrait painter about whom very little is known. He studied under Juan de las Roelas, painter of the great altarpiece at St. Isidore in Seville and the Martyrdom of St. Andrew in the Seville museum, and practised painting at Seville with indifferent success until about 1660, when he moved to Madrid for his remaining years.

His son and pupil Francisco Caro, born at Seville in 1627 and dead at Madrid in 1667, entered Alonso Cano's studio and considerably surpassed his father. His most important works show scenes from the life of Our Lady in the chapel of St. Isidore in St. Andrew's church, Madrid, and his largest painting, on the Portiuncula indulgence and jubilee for the Franciscan convent at Segovia, includes portraits of its donors, Senor and Senora de Contreras.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-piz:
Francisco Pizarro, born at Trujillo in Estremadura probably in 1471 and dead at Lima on 26 June 1541, was the illiterate conqueror of Peru. Illegitimate son of Gonzalo Pizarro, an infantry captain of the Neapolitan wars, and Francisca Gonzalez, who neglected his schooling, he grew up unable to read or write. Drawn by tales of Spanish exploits in America, he sailed in 1509 with Ojeda to Uraba and held San Sebastian for him. He joined Enciso at Cartagena and crossed Panama with Balboa to first sight the Pacific in 1513.

After Balboa's execution he served Pedrarias Davila, subdued tribes in Veraguas, and in 1522 heard accounts of a rich southern empire. With Diego de Almagro and the priest Hernando de Luque he planned the conquest of Peru and endured years of hardship. In 1532 he seized the Inca Atahuallpa at Cajamarca, holding him for ransom and then executing him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-sav:
Francisco Saverio Clavigero, born at Vera Cruz in Mexico on 9 September 1731 and dead at Bologna on 2 April 1787, was a Jesuit historian of ancient Mexico. Entering the Society at seventeen, he was directed by Father Campoi at the College of St. Peter and St. Paul in Mexico to the documents on Mexican history and antiquities collected by Siguenza y Gongora. He became an enthusiastic investigator. Expelled with the Jesuits from Mexico in 1767, he settled at Bologna, founded a literary academy, and pursued his documentary studies.

There he compiled his Ancient History of Mexico, published at Cesena in 1780, written against De Pauw, Raynal, and Robertson, who had belittled American peoples. Following Boturini, he listed sources with care for Indian pictographs on tissue and other materials and for Indian writers. His systematic arrangement, clear style, and sympathy for the conquered peoples won his book lasting favour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-galtelli-nuor:
Galtelli-Nuoro, a diocese in Sardinia's Sassari province, joins an old hill see with a highland town. Galtelli became a bishopric in 1138 under Innocent II, was suppressed by Alexander VI in 1495 and folded into Cagliari, then restored in 1787, though its bishop still lives at Nuoro. The diocese counts twenty-five parishes and 56,300 Catholics.

Nuoro, the ancient Nora, stands some 2,000 feet above the sea amid granite and lead quarries. Near it rise twenty-four Nuraghi, huge truncated cones of the Stone Age known as Giants' Tombs, wonders even to the ancients. Close by lie the Domos de Janas, rooms cut from living granite and linked together. Red jasper quarries and an old cathedral with fine paintings complete the picture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guigues-du-ch:
Guigues du Chastel, born in Dauphiné in 1083 or 1084, became fifth prior of the Grande Chartreuse in 1110 and gave the young Carthusian order its laws. When he took office only two charterhouses existed; nine more rose during his twenty-seven years. That growth forced him to write down the mother-house customs in his Consuetudines of 1127 or 1128.

After an avalanche wrecked the Grande Chartreuse in 1132 he rebuilt it on its present site. A learned organizer praised by St. Bernard and Peter the Venerable, he also wrote a life of St. Hugh of Grenoble, meditations, and letters, edited St. Jerome's letters in a lost edition, and is sometimes called Venerable, though the Bollandists found no trace of a formal cult.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-isernia-and-v:
Isernia, joined with Venafro as one diocese, sits in Molise between Monte Matese and Monte Azzo, on high ground near the Volturno in fertile country. In the Middle Ages it was famed for parchment making, a trade still carried on there. Ancient Aesernia ranked among the chief Samnite cities, fell to Rome in 295 before Christ. Stayed loyal through the Punic and Social wars until forced to yield in 90 before Christ after long resistance.

As the town decayed, Augustus and Nero planted colonies there. Roman remains survive: a bridge, aqueduct traces, and above all the lower courses of high walls in massive polygonal blocks, pre-Roman work. After Lombard invasion it became a countship under Benevento's duke. The entry gives a small Italian see the full weight of Samnite, Roman, and medieval layers beneath it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacopo-sannaz:
Italian and Latin poet Jacopo Sannazaro was born at Naples on 28 July 1458. He died at Rome in August 1530. His family was of Spanish origin and served Charles III of Durazzo. It held the fief of Rocca di Mondragone from the late fourteenth century. He took his name from St Nazarius, on whose feast he was born.

After losing his father young, he lived with his mother at Nocera dei Pagani. Returning to Naples, he studied with Pontanus and joined his academy. There he gained the name Sincerus, often used in letters of the time. He allied closely with Naples' Aragon princes. He followed Federico into exile after Louis XII of France drove him out in 1521. Federico settled at Tours on the French king's generosity. Sannazaro shared that exile and its literary world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jaro:
Jaro is a diocese in the Philippine Islands, formerly part of Cebú diocese. It became a separate diocese on 27 May 1865. It comprises Panay and Negros islands, the Romblon, Palawan, and Jolo groups, and on Mindanao the provinces of Zamboanga, Cotabato, and Davao. Its Catholic population exceeds one million. Here and there are some Aglipayan schismatics, and in Mindanao and Jolo many Muslims and some pagans.

In 1909 the diocese counted forty-five native priests, about forty Augustinian and Recollect friars, twenty Mill Hill missioners, and about ten Jesuits. In Jaro city a Lazarist-run diocesan seminary trains eighty students for priesthood, with the rest preparing for secular careers. At Iloilo city Augustinians run a college for lay students. Academies for young women stand at Jaro, Iloilo, Zamboanga, and Dumaguete. The entry presents a vast island diocese at work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-of-bicla:
John of Biclaro was a Visigothic chronicler whose history is the fullest and most reliable authority on King Leovigild's reign. Born in Portugal about the middle of the sixth century, he studied Latin and Greek at Constantinople for at least seven years. Returning home, he refused to join the Arian state church and was banished by Leovigild to Barcelona.

After Leovigild died in 586, John founded Biclaro's Benedictine monastery. He ruled it as abbot until he became Bishop of Gerona, attending synods at Saragossa in 592, Barcelona in 599, and Egara in 614. His chronicle, continuing Victor of Tunnuna from 567 to 590, tells the stormy story of the Visigothic conversion from Arianism to Catholicism with religious impartiality despite his own sufferings. Mommsen's 1893 edition remains the best.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-romero:
Juan Romero was a Spanish Jesuit missionary and authority on Guaraní. Born at Machena in Andalusia in 1559, he joined the Society of Jesus in 1580, reached Peru in January 1590, and served as superior of the Tucumán missions from 1593 to 1598. After serving as procurator in Rome, he returned in 1610.

Romero led the Jesuit colleges of Buenos Aires and Santiago del Estero and became first vice-provincial of Chile. In nearly forty years of mission work he gained fluent knowledge of several Indian tongues, above all Guaraní of Paraguay. He also left many letters, shorter papers, and a manuscript treatise on predestination. He died at Santiago, Chile, in 1630.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lorenzo-herva:
Lorenzo Hervas y Panduro was a Spanish Jesuit and famed student of languages, born at Horcajo in 1735 and dead at Rome in 1809. He taught in Madrid and Murcia, served as a missionary in America until the Jesuits were expelled in 1767, and then settled in Italy.

At Cesena and Rome he met Jesuits driven from every corner of the world. He mined their knowledge of remote tongues no books could teach. His huge Idea dell' Universo ran to twenty-one volumes. Its Catalogue of Languages, issued 1800 to 1805, traced peoples by speech: American tongues first, then Pacific island tongues, then Europe's, which he judged weaker.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luis-cancer-d:
Luis Cancer de Barbastro was a Dominican missionary, born in Aragon at an unknown date and killed at Tampa Bay about 1549. One of the first Dominicans to follow Las Casas to Guatemala, he laboured among Vera Paz Indians with zeal and courage.

He wrote songs in Zapotec on the mysteries of faith for Vera Paz converts, a manuscript now lost to view. A staunch ally of Las Casas, he backed him at the Mexico gathering of 1546, then won from Spain charge of converting Florida Indians by peaceful means. Sailing from Vera Cruz in 1549 with two fellow Dominicans, he was betrayed by their interpreter Magdalen, and all three priests were slain on reaching shore.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mayotte-nossi:
The prefecture apostolic of Mayotte, Nossi-Be, and Comoro covers the Comoro archipelago, the Satellites of Madagascar. Mayotte, the farthest south and most important of the Comoros, stands with Anjuan, Mohilla, and Great Comoro, plus Nossi-Be and Santa Maria. The islands look like cones of drowned groves, cut from the mainland by deep gulfs.

Heights run from Mayotte's 1,800 feet to Anjuan's 5,000 and Great Comoro's volcanic cone above 7,000. Two monsoons bring two seasons, sometimes with cyclones, and the rich soil yields vanilla, cloves, sugar cane, and coffee in plenty. Some 80,000 people live there, mostly Africans, with Sakalavas from Madagascar. The group was for centuries an Arab colony, once very prosperous, and the entry maps its lands, peoples, and church charge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-melchior-carn:
Melchior Carneiro, a missionary bishop born of a noble Coimbra family, died at Macao in 1583. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1543, became first rector of Evora College in 1551, and soon after took the Lisbon rectorship. When Simon Rodriguez, Portugal's first provincial, was called to Rome to answer charges, the visitor Nadal gave him Carneiro as companion.

King John of Portugal had asked Pope Julius III and St. Ignatius for a Jesuit Patriarch of Ethiopia. The pope chose John Nunez, with Andrew Oviedo and Carneiro as coadjutors with right of succession. Consecrated in 1555, they were the first Jesuits raised to the episcopate. Ignatius accepted, judging the rank a burden of hardship rather than honour. Barred from Ethiopia, Carneiro laboured at Goa and on the Malabar coast until 1567, when he became first bishop of Japan and China, an office he soon gave up.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-montefeltro:
Montefeltro, in the province of Urbino in the Marches, first appears as Mona Feretri in the diplomas by which Charlemagne confirmed Pepin's grants to the Holy See. Its counts became imperial vicars in 1135 and Counts of Urbino in 1213, though their rule was broken between 1322 and 1375, and Cardinal Albornoz expelled them again in 1359.

The elder Guido of Montefeltro, a famed Ghibelline captain, ended his life as a Franciscan in 1298. Its first known bishop, Agatho, sat at San Leo in 826, and later bishops built the cathedral, the episcopal palace at Calamello and the seminary at Pennabilli, where the see eventually settled. The diocese, suffragan of Urbino, follows its bishops and shifting seats through the centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-montenegro:
Montenegro is a kingdom on the Adriatic's east coast in the Balkans, once part of Roman Dalmatia. Diocletian carved out the province of Praevalis there, with Dioclea as capital. From the seventh century Serb tribes settled the land, founding principalities called zupanates. The southernmost was Zeta, later Duklja, cradle of the Nemanjic family.

Stefan I Nemanja, recognised as chief zupan in 1165, embraced Orthodoxy and organised the Serbian Church. His son Sava, first Orthodox Archbishop of Serbia in 1221, founded a see for Zeta near Cattaro. Under Stefan Dusan the Balsic family governed Zeta, then the Crnojevic line resisted them. After the Serbian Empire fell, the mountain land kept its independence against Turks and Venetians, with its prince-bishops and later kings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nero:
Nero, the last Julian-Claudian emperor, reigned from 54 to 68 as son of Domitius Ahenobarbus and Julia Agrippina, niece of Claudius. After Messalina's violent death, Claudius married Julia, adopted her son Nero, and gave him his daughter Octavia in marriage. Agrippina, ready for any crime to enthrone her son, had Seneca made his tutor and Burrus commander of the Praetorian guard.

Born at Antium on 15 December 37, Nero was seventeen at his accession, believing himself a great singer and poet, his better nature stifled by sensuality and moral perversity. Agrippina hoped to share his rule, but her autocratic temper soon ended that. His first years, directed by Burrus and Seneca, the real holders of power, were auspicious, easing taxation and provincial abuses. The entry follows his later crimes, the fire of Rome, persecution of Christians, and his fall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicastro:
Nicastro is a city of Catanzaro province in Calabria, southern Italy, on a promontory commanding the Gulf of Saint Euphemia, with an ancient castle above. Its port exports acid, herbs and wine. The cathedral, an ancient temple, with the episcopal palace, stood outside the city. Saracens pillaged it, it was restored in 1100, then destroyed in the 1638 earthquake with the palace, losing most valuable archives under the ruins.

The Greek Rite long prevailed at Nicastro. Its first recorded bishop was Henry in 1090. Tancredo da Monte Foscolo, deposed by Honorius IV for crowning John of Aragon King of Sicily, was reinstated by Boniface VIII. Paolo Capisucco judged Henry VIII's marriage case, Marcello Cervino became Pope Marcellus II, and Giovanni Tommaso Perrone built the new cathedral. In 1818 Martorano joined the diocese, suffragan of Reggio, with 52 parishes and 110,100 people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pesaro:
Pesaro was an Adriatic city at the Foglia's mouth, living by fishing, farming, majolica, and mining. Its cathedral of San Francesco carries a Gothic portal and Bellini's Coronation of the Madonna, while San Domenico holds the tomb of the poet Giulio Perticari. The Ducal Palace, begun by Laurana before 1465, and the Almerici museum of inscriptions, coins, ivories, and majolica anchor its civic pride.

Senones held the town until Rome drove them out in 283 BC, and it became a colony in 184. Gothic War sieges battered it, Lombards took it four times, and it passed to the Papal States. Malatesta lords gave way to the Sforza, when Galeazzo Malatesta settled Pesaro as dower on his niece Costanza Varano. Rossini, born here, is honoured by its music school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-piero-da-san-:
Piero della Francesca was the great realist painter of the early Renaissance, born at Borgo San Sepolcro about 1420. Son of the notary Ser Benedetto, he worked at Perugia in 1438, probably under Domenico Veneziano, and at Sant'Egidio in Florence in 1439 and 1440. Domenico and Paolo Uccello shaped his art. He emerged as an independent master in 1445 with a many-panelled altarpiece for his town's Misericordia brotherhood.

At Rimini in 1451 he painted Sigismondo Malatesta venerating his patron, and between about 1460 and 1466 he created his masterpiece, the Arezzo choir frescoes of the True Cross. His Resurrection at Borgo, his Baptism and moonlit Nativity in London, and his perspective treatise, Prospettiva Pingendi, made him the age's master of perspective and light. Perugino's generation learned from him. He died at home in 1492.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-policastro:
Policastro is a diocese in the province of Salerno in southern Italy, on a hill above the gulf that bears its name. It is the ancient Pituntia and continues the Diocese of Buxentum, whose first known bishop was Rusticus in 501. It is suffragan to Salerno and counts thirty-eight parishes with 64,000 people.

Its bishops include Gabriele Atilio, a Latin poet of 1471, and Urbano Felicio, who held a synod in 1630. Vincenzo de Sylva, besieged in his palace by Count Carafa for defending church rights, remodelled the see, while Tommaso and Antonio della Rosa restored cathedral and seminary.
