The present bishop at the entry's writing was Mgr. Vescia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-queretaro:
Queretaro, a diocese in Mexico under Michoacan, covers the state of the same name: 4,492 square miles, with 243,515 people by the census of 1910. This encyclopedia entry names its chief city, home of bishop and governor, as Querétaro itself, with 35,011 people in 1910. Otomi Indians founded the city in 1446, and Spaniards have held it since 1531. Religious orders arrived in turn: Carmelites in 1601, Dieguinos in 1613, Fathers of Mercy in 1636, and Dominicans in 1692.

Augustinians and Fathers of the Oratory of Saint Philip also kept houses there. The Jesuit college of Saint Francis Xavier fell in 1767, when Charles the Third expelled all Jesuits from Spanish lands. One institution outshone the rest: the college of Apostolic missionaries, which Innocent the Eleventh called the greatest influence for spreading the faith, sending missioners far beyond Mexico, even to Upper California. Vera, Noriega and Domenech supply the entry's Mexican sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raimundo-dios:
Raimundo Diosdado Caballero, miscellaneous writer chiefly on church topics, was born at Palma in Majorca on 19 June 1740. This encyclopedia entry gives his death at Rome uncertainly, as either 16 January 1830 or 28 April 1829. He entered the Society of Jesus on 15 November 1752. He held the literature chair at the Jesuit College in Madrid for several years. He was deported to Italy with the other Jesuits when the Society was suppressed in Spanish lands.

In his new home Father Caballero pursued a varied literary career. His chief works include a study of the first age of Spanish printing, printed at Rome in 1793, and critical notes of 1798 that correct Schelstrate and Hardouin. In the latter he argues that the native tongue of Christ and the Apostles was Syriac, not Greek, against Dominicus Diodati. Later writings treat Mexican history, closer union between American and European Spaniards, and American considerations, with Sommervogel and Hurter as sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rio-negro:
Rio Negro was a prefecture apostolic in Brazil, carved from the See of Amazones by a decree of October 1910. It was bounded on the south by the watershed between the Rio Negro and the Rio Branco. On other sides lay Colombia and Venezuela and the territory of Rio Branco. The white population was small, confined to a few villages along the Rio Negro itself.

Mission history reaches back to 1658, when the Jesuit Francisco Gonsales founded a mission for the peoples of the Upper Rio Negro. Traces of Jesuit work still survived in scattered villages. A Carmelite evangelized the Tucumaos two years later. From 1870 the Franciscans laboured among the Indians, with seven stations on the Uaupes, four on the Tikie, and one on the Papuri. When the empire fell, most missions were abandoned, though some were later restored.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-san-severo:
San Severo, a diocese in Foggia province in southern Italy, lies on a fertile plain watered by the Radicosa and Triolo rivers. Its city's origin is obscure. Under the Normans it housed a prince, then passed to the Benedictines of Torre Maggiore and later to the Templars, whose suppression broke up its lands. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a see through earthquakes and transfers.

Quakes struck hard in 1627, 1828, and 1851. The diocese, set up in 1580, merely continues Civitate, which itself succeeded ancient Teanum. At Civitate papal troops lost to the Normans in 1052, and its bishops included the theologian Lorenzo da Viterbo, the astronomer Luca Gaurico, and Francesco Alciato, later cardinal. Martino de Martini, a Jesuit, became San Severo's first bishop in 1580.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-santiago-del-:
Santiago del Estero, an Argentine diocese erected on 25 March 1907 as suffragan of Buenos Aires, exactly matches its home state. It is bounded by Salta, Tucumán, La Rioja, Córdoba, Santa Fe, and the Chaco territory. It covers nearly 40,000 square miles with about five people per square mile. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia notes a paradox: the newest diocese holds the oldest see.

Santiago city, on the Dulce river forty miles north of the Great Salt Marshes, hosted the first bishop in that part of South America. Church organisation in the future Argentina began in 1570 under Pius V, who erected the diocese of Tucumán over a vast, barely explored land. The entry follows that original diocese's slow division into the modern sees of the north-west.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sao-sebastiao:
São Sebastião do Rio de Janeiro, the ecclesiastical province of Rio, third of Brazil's seven, began as a bishopric under São Salvador da Bahia by a bull of 22 November 1676. It became an archbishopric in 1893, ruling Niterói, Espírito Santo, and the Rio Branco prefecture. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia counts a province of two million Catholics.

The whole province held 2,051,800 Catholics in 1910, with 800,000 in the archdiocese proper, which covers the federal district where Rio, the republic's capital, stands. Twenty parish churches, fifty-nine chapels, monasteries, nunneries, and sixty-three Catholic associations serve the district. Chief among them is the Candelaria brotherhood of the Blessed Sacrament, founded in 1669, which runs charities caring for nearly a thousand poor people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-socorro:
Established in 1895 as a suffragan see, Socorro arose at Chiancon, the settlement of an Indian chief of the same name, defeated and captured by Martin Galeano in 1540. The village moved to its present site in 1681 under Our Lady of Succour, won parish rank in 1683, and was definitively built eight years later. It rose to town rank in 1771.

Socorro counts among the first cities in Colombia's independence movement, revolting against Spanish authorities as late as 1781. It serves as capital of its province in the Department of Santander. The present bishop, at the entry's writing, is Evaristo Blanco.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-seraphin-o:
Seraphin of Montegranaro, a Capuchin lay brother, gave unlettered counsel that bishops and princes sought. Born Felix de Nicola at Montegranaro in 1540 to a poor, pious family, he worked as a shepherd in youth, with long leisure for prayer. After his parents died, his eldest brother treated him harshly and cruelly.

At sixteen he entered the Capuchin Friars Minor and took the name Seraphin. He stood out for simplicity, mortification, obedience, and boundless charity to the poor. He loved the Eucharist and Our Lady, read hearts, and worked miracles and prophecy. Though unlettered, his advice proved a fruitful source of virtue. He died at Ascoli on 12 October 1604 and was canonised in 1767.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tomas-camara-:
Tomas Camara y Castro, Bishop of Salamanca, was born at Torrecilla de Cameros in 1847 and died at Villaharta in 1904. His father was the town physician. Tomas studied humanities at Burgos, took the Augustinian habit at Valladolid at fifteen, finished his theology there, and became professor in the college. His energy seemed inexhaustible.

As bishop he founded the Colegio de Calatrava at Salamanca, built a handsome church to St. John of Sahagun, patron of the city, and raised six smaller churches elsewhere. Above all he was a polemicist and orator, prominent in congresses, the Senate and the press, and beloved by Catholics. His Lenten conferences of 1884 and 1885 drew the leading men of letters, politics, science and art.
cicero:
Cicero, by W. Lucas Collins, is a life and study of the Roman orator written for a series on the ancient classics. The author's preface note signs itself W.L.C. and owns the translations as his own work. Twelve chapters carry the book from Cicero's schooling to his religion.

Public life fills the middle chapters: the impeachment of Verres, the consulship and Catiline, exile and return, then Cicero set against Caesar and Antony in turn. Later chapters judge his character as politician and orator. His correspondence gets a chapter of its own. The essays on old age and friendship, his philosophy, and his religion close the study.
doe-osti-17014394-release-of-evaluated-m:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-26-28560, issued September 24, 2026, documents new nuclear data for the ENDF/B-IX.0 library. Denise Neudecker and five coauthors evaluated average prompt fission neutron counts, called nu values, for minor uranium isotopes 232 through 234 and 236. Such data feed reactor and criticality safety calculations.

For each isotope the team picked one of four candidate evaluations, favoring fits to measured data and smooth trends. Picks were then checked against hundreds of test assemblies by watching a key multiplication factor. The minor isotope picks changed that factor by no more than 12 pcm, a tiny unit. The related uranium 233 pick shifted some test results far more.
doe-osti-2571174-innovative-polyhydroxya:
Final technical report DE-EE0009268, led by Stephanie Lansing of the University of Maryland, covers work from October 2020 to March 2025. Partners were Idaho National Laboratory, Virginia Tech, Quasar Energy Group, and the Naval Research Laboratory. The goal was to turn food waste into PHA bioplastics instead of landfill gas. The route reroutes a standard waste process at its middle step.

Food waste first goes through dark fermentation, which breaks it into short carbon chains called volatile fatty acids. Methane making is then blocked on purpose, saving those acids for Haloferax mediterranei, a salt-loving microbe that converts them into plastic. Microbial electrochemical cells boosted acid output and shaped the plastic type. Overall carbon conversion passed 50 percent, disposal costs fell by more than 25 percent, and a 50 liter pilot reactor ran PHA production for over 100 hours.
doe-osti-2586693-towards-exact-finite-te:
James Shepherd of the University of Iowa wrote this final technical report for Department of Energy award DE-SC0021317, covering September 2020 through December 2023. The project worked toward exact electronic structure calculations at finite temperature for solids and molecules. Heat changes how electrons behave, and most standard methods assume away that problem.

The team's main tool is density matrix quantum Monte Carlo, a method that simulates the electron density matrix directly. Shepherd's group made it faster and more accurate, and built the work into HANDE-QMC, an open-source software package shared with the wider field. Benchmarks compared the method against full configuration interaction results for small molecules such as methane and water. Machine learning helped pull thermodynamic properties out of the simulation data. The project produced seven peer-reviewed papers, then moved to Michigan State University to continue.
doe-osti-2588046-sup-193-sup-mir-sup-192:
Gencho Rusev, Athena Marenco, Evelyn Bond, and Todd Bredeweg of Los Alamos National Laboratory wrote this report, LA-UR-25-22344, dated July 23, 2025. It measures a ratio of two iridium isotopes made by neutron irradiation: the metastable iridium-193m against iridium-192. Such ratios act as fingerprints of the neutron spectrum that produced them, which is why critical assembly operators care.

Eight irradiations of potassium iridium chloride pellets were carried out on three critical assemblies. The machines, all at the National Criticality Experiments Research Center, were Flattop with a uranium core, Flattop with a plutonium core, and Godiva IV. One run placed three pellets at different spots in an assembly to map how the ratio shifts with position. The samples were then counted to extract the isotope production. The results give spectrum watchers a calibrated marker across three of the center's best-known machines.
doe-osti-2588408-chemical-and-optical-co:
Robert Baker's final technical report closes award DE-SC0020977 from the Department of Energy's Office of Science. The project built and used extreme ultraviolet spectroscopy to watch charge, spin, and solvation in molecules and at interfaces. Sum frequency generation vibrational spectroscopy served as a second probe. The hosted text carries light character noise, but its findings read clearly.

Achievements fall in three areas. First, ultrafast XUV reflection spectroscopy measured how electrons and holes relax and get trapped at titanium dioxide surfaces. The measurements covered both above-band-gap ultraviolet and below-band-gap visible light. They also showed how oxygen vacancy defects speed hole trapping. Second, the work moved to molecular magnets. It tackled the pentanuclear cluster Co3Fe2, which flips spin states after a light-induced metal-to-metal charge transfer. Third, the methods were pushed toward spin crossover in native solvation, the setting such molecules actually work in.
doe-osti-2589874-pi-extended-porphyrins-:
University of North Texas final report on award DE-SC0016766, led by Hong Wang with Francis D'Souza, covers a Basic Energy Sciences project on oversized porphyrin molecules. Porphyrins are ring-shaped, carbon-rich molecules related to the pigments in blood and leaves. Stretching the ring system outward changes how the molecule handles light and electrons, which suits it for molecular electronics.

The laboratory's main task was synthesis: making these stretched rings at all had been a bottleneck. New concise routes fused extra ring systems onto the porphyrin edge, including fused aromatic blocks, oxygen- and nitrogen-bearing rings, antiaromatic parts, and cross-linked parts. Push-pull versions, with electron donors on one side and acceptors on the other, were also built. Linked pairs and triples of rings let the team steer energy and electron flow, a control need shared with solar cells and batteries.
doe-osti-2997544-electron-cloud-predicti:
Brookhaven National Laboratory technical note BNL-229019-2025-TECH, also numbered EIC-ADD-TN-148, by Silvia Verdu-Andres, predicts electron cloud trouble in the Electron-Ion Collider's Hadron Storage Ring. Stray electrons knocked from the vacuum chamber walls can multiply into a cloud that shakes the beam. The note models that build-up and lists the planned countermeasures.

Stability studies center on the 275 GeV proton beam at top luminosity, with 60 millimeter bunch length. Calculations assume the electron cloud in its saturated state and a beam screen surface with a secondary emission yield of 1.1, the factor for how many electrons each impact frees. Electron density near the beam right after a bunch passes is treated as uniform, and its level hinges on that surface yield. Coatings and surface choices that hold the yield down are the practical lever.
doe-osti-2999095-machine-learning-guided:
Le Thanh Mai Pham, Ryan Bruneau, Jimmy Yuan and co-workers at Sandia National Laboratories close project CB11459 in final report SAND2025-12321R, covering August 2024 to August 2025. The goal was readiness for Disease X, a future unknown pathogen. Their method uses machine learning to pick antibodies likely to block a broad range of related viruses, by aiming at epitopes, the surface patches antibodies grip, that stay alike across variants.

A transfer learning framework carried models trained on one virus across to its relatives. In the main case, models taught on the SARS-CoV-2 spike were retrained for SARS-CoV-1, using shared binding-domain windows. Shared epitope patches kept their predictive power, and contact hotspots were mapped for antibody design. Models handled antibodies they had never seen, and checks against held-out test data matched experiments well. The project delivered a pipeline that finds and ranks such patches.
doe-osti-3000131-development-of-a-flex-f:
Marquette University's final report for award DE-EE0009872, led by Professor Adam Dempsey, covers April 2022 to June 2025 and a new way to burn gasoline-ethanol blends cleanly. The system pairs a prechamber, a small side pocket where a spark first lights a rich mixture, with mixing-controlled combustion in the main chamber. Flex-fuel engines must handle any blend from plain gasoline to high ethanol, and this design aims for diesel-like efficiency on those fuels.

Work ran from bench science to a running multi-cylinder engine. Optical rapid-compression machine tests and modelling came first, then offset prechamber tests with surface temperature readings. A prototype prechamber was designed and machined, proven on a single-cylinder engine, and an operating strategy was tuned. Finally a multi-cylinder demonstration engine was built and run in the laboratory. A techno-economic analysis closes the report, weighing the concept's cost against its gains.
doe-osti-3009502-the-measurement-of-grai:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2025-15206, by Alan Jankowski, Meghan Rogers, and Joshua Yee, printed December 2025, examines how measured grain size depends on the settings of electron backscatter diffraction. The test material is a thin-wall 316L stainless steel section built by additive manufacturing.

At a 2 degree misorientation threshold, the average grain size read 10.30 micrometres in an 800-times scan with 176 nanometre pixels. The same threshold at 2000-times magnification and 30 nanometre pixels read 4.68 micrometres, but the finer map took 350 minutes against 59.5. Grain size numbers, the report shows, are meaningless without the scan conditions attached.
doe-osti-3013610-quantum-monte-carlo-and:
Kenneth Nollett of San Diego State University wrote this final technical report for award DE-SC0019257, covering September 2018 to August 2024. The project advanced quantum Monte Carlo methods for computing how particles scatter from light atomic nuclei. These calculations, built from protons and neutrons directly, feed astrophysics, where reaction rates inside stars are hard to measure in the lab.

The main thrust extended Monte Carlo wave functions to coupled-channel scattering, starting with neutron-triton scattering using the variational Monte Carlo method. A second thrust developed integral methods that extract scattering properties from bound-state-like calculations. Nollett also co-led a working group in the Solar Fusion III review, covering the helium-3 reactions that power the sun and set the solar neutrino rates experiments observe.
doe-osti-3015671-icl-commercial-producti:
An ICL Specialty Products final report under award DE-MS0000012, dated February 2, 2026, accounts for a lithium iron phosphate cathode powder plant. The project spent 24,255,499 dollars in total. The DOE share was 8,817,536 dollars, and the rest was company cost share. The spending covered plant design, permits, and readiness for a 30,000-ton-scale facility.

Laboratory work synthesized the cathode powder from iron powder at seven-kilogram scale. It used the licensed method. A shorter production route cut plant capital cost by more than 20 million dollars in value engineering. Equipment specifications, environmental permits, hazard analysis, and long-lead procurement all advanced. The project was then cancelled before the construction budget period. The plant was never built.
doe-osti-3017972-act-university-collabor:
Daniel Whisler, Amanda Wu, and Matt Nelms of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory wrote this February 2026 final report for an ACT university collaboration. Amanda Wu was the laboratory principal investigator. The project asked how manufacturing defects change material failure under dynamic loading, fast, violent stress of the kind parts see in extreme service. Work fed enhanced failure models for programs including W87-1 and depleted uranium modernization.

Experiments and simulations validated the models under a variety of extreme loading conditions, starting from parts with known initial defects. Partner testing ran at the University of California San Diego. One surprise: necked specimens showed unexpected stress-strain behavior in yield and ultimate stress. After accounting for different starting gauge lengths, the two test curves should have overlapped, and did not. Findings like that are exactly what failure modelers need, because a model that only fits clean specimens will lie about real hardware.
doe-osti-3020531-development-of-biofuel-:
National Laboratory of the Rockies CRADA final report NLR/TP-2700-98764, CRD-18-00765 (Project 2), with Lieve Laurens as technical contact, reports algae biofuel research done with partner EMRE. Turning carbon dioxide into fuel with photosynthetic algae first requires high photosynthetic efficiency. This project attacked the biological bottlenecks, and the practical gap between laboratory cultivation and outdoor production, that limit bio-oil yield.

Researchers compared two variants of the alga P. celeri, using genetic and biochemical profiling to find why one uses light energy better. Cultures acclimated to high light were tested with chemical inhibitors to map how excess energy is shed as heat, a safety valve called non-photochemical quenching. Findings pointed to shifts in the balance between ATP and NADPH production during rapid growth. The results inform stakeholders designing a sustainable algae biofuel supply chain.
doe-osti-3022913-preparing-california-s-:
LLNL report LLNL-TR-2008241, by Caspar Donnison and Roger Aines, prepares California's cap-and-trade program for the state's 2045 carbon neutrality law. The arithmetic of the mandate frames the paper. An 85 percent cut in greenhouse gases below 1990 levels by 2045 leaves roughly 15 percent, about 65 million tonnes. Carbon dioxide removal must balance that share.

The report explains how removal could be integrated into the trading system without repeating the weaknesses of conventional offsets. Offsets pay for emissions avoided elsewhere. They vary widely in quality depending on whether the carbon is fossil or atmospheric. Policy steps include implementing SB 905 to formalize agency roles in permitting carbon management infrastructure. They also include coordinating with the Low Carbon Fuel Standard, which already lets fuel producers buy removal credits.
doe-osti-3024110-probing-dynamic-phase-c:
Y Shirley Meng, then at the University of California San Diego, reports award DE-FG02-10ER46672 for July 2020 through July 2024, dated July 15, 2024. Meng moved to the University of Chicago in February 2022 and kept an unpaid San Diego adjunct post under a transition plan. The science uses cryogenic and in situ analytical electron microscopy to watch phase changes inside electrochemical materials as they happen.

Targets include the resistive state changes in solid-state materials proposed for non-volatile, neuromorphic memory. Worked analysis goes deep into manganese chemistry: Mn3+ ions in oxygen octahedra split their d-electrons between t2g and eg levels, and the unequal eg electron stretches the octahedron along one axis. Such atomic-scale distortions are exactly what the microscopy program was built to connect to device behavior.
doe-osti-3030660-advanced-materials-for-:
Richard E. Wirz of the University of California, Los Angeles, led the AMPERE project under ARPA-E award DE-AR0001378, within the GAMOW fusion program. The reporting period ran from February 2021 to February 2024, and Oregon State University shared the work. AMPERE stands for Advanced Materials for Plasma-Exposed Robust Electrodes. Electrodes facing fusion plasma erode fast, which caps device life. The team built a new class of electrode stock to fight that wear.

Their answer is volumetrically complex materials, porous metal foams tuned by plasma-material interaction science. The report claims strong gains in device performance and longevity from the foams. High-power plasma tests ran in the lab Large Plasma Device, with its standard diagnostics plus optical checks and witness plates. Setup for those tests finished late in 2022, after some delay.
doe-osti-3031039-exotic-uses-of-neutrons:
Dustin Allen Gilbert of the University of Tennessee closes an Early Career award, DE-SC0021344, that ran from September 2020 to August 2025. The project used neutrons and X-rays as probes of chiral magnets, materials whose magnetic moments curl instead of lining up straight. Some curled patterns close into loops called skyrmions. A skyrmion cannot be smoothed away without a break, which gives it particle-like behavior and possible uses in memory devices.

Neutrons were the first tool ever used to spot skyrmions, and they stay a gold standard. The team showed neutrons can read skyrmions in gadolinium-iron multilayer films, the only clear thin-film case measured that way, per the report. Most neutron work needs bulky samples, since neutrons interact weakly, so a film result widens what the method can reach.
doe-osti-3374867-evaluation-of-commercia:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL/TAPS-26/3 evaluates vehicle-to-home systems that buyers can purchase today. Sam Thurston and Payas Dinesh Vartak wrote it for Argonne. Barney Richard Carlson of Idaho National Laboratory joins them. The work sits in the V2X Connect project. Vehicle-to-home gear lets an electric truck or car feed a house during an outage. Each brand's kit is closed and proprietary, so the team tested whole systems as sold.

One test pushed a Tesla Powershare unit past its rated backup output. That rating is 240 volts AC at 48 amps, or 11.5 kilowatts. When home demand crossed the line, the unit shut backup power off in full. It kept polling the load while tripped. Once demand fell back inside the rating, the unit restored power on its own. The report tracks that behavior in both real and staged outages.
doe-osti-3376150-nw-brave-t3-hydroplane-:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory close-out report PNNL-39468, by Connah G. Johnson and David D. Pollock and published in June 2026, wraps up the T3 Hydroplane analysis under the NW-BRaVE program. Hydroplane is a computing method for viral genome scans. It hunts for shared blocks across many genomes. It groups short sequence pieces, called kmers, by position inside local clusters called storms, not by plain similarity.

A run needs at least three matching kmers to bound a storm. Gaps between matched kmers are held to plus or minus three bases. Keeping the offset loose at this stage skips costly re-alignment work. The team tested the clouds against a set of one hundred nine genomes. A large share of sites lit up under the scan. The close-out frames that reach, and the spread of segment types found, as the proof the method scales.
doe-osti-3379845-scale-up-production-of-:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2026/4485, dated July 2025, investigates scaling up carbon fiber production from petroleum mesophase pitch. Six authors are printed: Merlin Theodore, Tom Holcombe, Chris Boyer, Daniel Webb, Jason Newport, and Sefa Yilmaz. The pitch came from Advanced Carbon Products Technologies, which uses a patented process to turn petroleum pitch into a carbon-rich feedstock.

Pitch-based carbon fibers promise cost-effective, high-performance material for structural and high-modulus composites, but precursor handling and scale-up have limited their use. The team developed processing criteria for the tailored mesophase pitch and demonstrated that it can be processed into precursor and carbon fiber at scale. A side benefit is carbon storage: the carbon in the fiber is locked into products instead of being burned and released.
doe-osti-3384942-scale-up-production-of-:
Scale Up Production of Carbon Fibers from Petroleum Mesophase Pitch, Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2026/4485 dated July 2025, examines whether a specialty pitch can become a fiber feedstock at production scale. Merlin Theodore, Tom Holcombe, Chris Boyer, Daniel Webb, Jason Newport, and Sefa Yilmaz are the printed team. The mesophase pitch was formulated by Advanced Carbon Products Technologies under its patented processing technology.

The abstract lays out the result. The process converts petroleum pitch into a high-value, low-cost, carbon-rich feedstock for carbon fiber and other materials the report calls critical to national security. Processing criteria for the tailored pitch were developed, and its conversion into precursor and then carbon fiber was demonstrated at scale. Tailored isotropic and mesophase materials were both evaluated, against the standing problem that pitch fibers promise cheap, stiff composites but resist scale-up.
doe-osti-3399499-non-intrusive-load-moni:
A preliminary study of non-intrusive load monitoring for electron beam welding processes, Los Alamos report LA-UR-26-26853 issued July 31, 2026, was performed by R. Bruce Madigan and Michael David McAninch of Gray Beards Engineering. They worked for Mark Joseph Cola of the laboratory, under a contract dated November 19, 2024. The idea borrows from building energy work. Read a machine's power draw and infer what the process is doing, without touching the process.

The main question is whether induced off-nominal disturbances can be spotted inside the welding machine's input power data. The preliminary work built familiarity. A PIPPES acquisition system sampled at 12,000 samples per second, triggered by the welding control program. The team recorded three-phase input power beside the machine's own diagnostics: beam voltage, focus current, and stigmator settings. The machine was a Probeam welding machine. The two records could therefore be correlated.
doe-osti-3399503-non-intrusive-load-moni:
A second study of non-intrusive load monitoring for electron beam welding, Los Alamos report LA-UR-26-26894 issued August 3, 2026, was performed by R. Bruce Madigan and Michael David McAninch of Gray Beards Engineering for Mark Joseph Cola, under the same contract as the first; the study itself is dated July 3, 2025. It asks whether four induced welding disturbances can be seen in the input power feeding the electron gun's high-voltage cabinet.

The disturbances are named: beam arc-out on a high vapor pressure aluminum plate, pulsed beam voltage, pulsed beam current, and pulsed beam focus current. The method improved on the first study's weak point. One PIPPES acquisition system now records machine input power and all process outputs together, beam deflection, focus, stigmators, alignment, voltage, and current, ending the synchronization trouble that two separate instruments caused before.
doe-osti-3422007-application-of-machine-:
Report NLR/TP-2800-99676 from the National Laboratory of the Rockies, dated August 2026, applies machine learning to making glucaric acid from biological feedstocks. Violeta Sanchez i Nogue was the lab contact. Glucaric acid is a sugar-derived chemical with many product uses.

A bioreactor campaign tested batch and fed glucose effects on output. Bioreactors are slow, so the number of runs and repeats stayed limited. That limit is also a strength: data came from the normal process, not a shrunk stand-in. Models trained on real process data can guide the next runs toward higher yields.
doe-osti-3422605-life-cycle-inventory-da:
Argonne report ANL-26/39, dated August 2026, supplies life cycle data for making renewable natural gas from corn stover and stillage. Ulises R. Gracida-Alvarez, Branden E. Leonhardt, and Longwen Ou are among the authors. Anaerobic digestion turns the wet waste into biogas.

One assumption sets a dry mass ratio of one to one between grain stillage and dried distillers grains. About 0.0714 dry tons of that feed are given up per unit of raw biogas. The choice does not change the ethanol product's carbon score in their setup. Fuel analysts get traceable numbers for judging this waste-to-gas path.
doe-osti-3904546-crosscutting-machine-le:
Livermore report LLNL-TR-2024716, dated September 2026, closes a directed research project on machine learning for particle physics. Jason Brodsky is the sole printed author, and the project code is 24-ERD-002. Most learning work in the field classifies collisions or measures particle energies. Brodsky's team instead built two methods meant to travel across experiments. One cleans noisy detector signals with only partial labels. The other infers hidden parameters from simulation sets.

The cleaning method was proven on xenon signals for the planned nEXO detector hunting a rare decay. A journal paper on it appeared in 2026. The inference method targeted Higgs physics beyond the standard model at the Large Hadron Collider, with a paper forthcoming. Both methods were chosen for reach: they fed six proposals to a 2026 mission call, two of which won funding. The report is short by design, a final summary rather than a technical archive.
euthyphro:
Plato's Euthyphro, in Benjamin Jowett's translation, meets Socrates outside the king archon's court, where he awaits trial for impiety. Euthyphro, a self-certain diviner, is prosecuting his own father for murder and claims to know exactly what piety is. Socrates begs for the standard by which all actions may be measured.

Each definition fails in turn. Piety is prosecuting wrongdoers, then what gods love, then part of justice. Then the famous question lands: is the pious loved because it is pious, or pious because loved? Jowett's introduction notes Plato puts the accusers, not Socrates, on trial here. The short dialogue founded two thousand years of argument about religion and morality.
government-and-rebellion-a-sermon-delive:
On Sunday morning, April 28, 1861, the Reverend E. E. Adams preached this sermon at the North Broad Street Presbyterian Church, and it was published by request. The nation had just split; Fort Sumter had fallen two weeks before. His text is Proverbs, chapter seventeen, verse eleven: an evil man seeketh only rebellion, and a cruel messenger shall be sent against him. Adams takes the verse as a plain announcement.

Rebellion, he argues, is a crime that God will judge, and the conscience of man agrees. As God does not pardon the rebel who will not repent, so the state must assert its majesty. The sermon is a Union plea from a Northern pulpit at the war's first heat. It shows how ministers framed secession as sin, and duty to the Union as duty to God.
grappling-with-the-monster-or-the-curse-:
T. S. Arthur, famed for Ten Nights in a Bar-Room, calls strong drink the Monster in this temperance volume. His introduction says the mass of matter that came to his hands left him with the hard task of choosing and cutting down. There is not a chapter, he claims, that might not have been twice as long. A front picture shows a victim in the monster's clutches, body and brain on fire.

Arthur mixes tales of ruined homes with facts on drink, law, and the body. His cure is total abstinence, pressed by moral force and by statute. The book argues, pleads, and warns in turn. It belongs to the great wave of temperance print that swept America in the late 1800s. As a record of how that cause was argued to plain readers, it is full and forceful.
history-of-the-expedition-to-russia-unde:
Count Philippe de Ségur, a general who marched with Napoleon, wrote this history of the 1812 expedition to Russia. The hosted copy is the first volume of a revised second edition, at London in 1825. Ségur dedicates the work to the veterans of the Grand Army. He tells them their lives now rest in great recollections.

Moscow's emptying astounds even the invaders in his telling. Nobles, tradesmen, and laborers all fled alike, he writes. Two volumes, a map, and seven engravings made up the set. Ségur writes as witness and mourner at once. Readers get the most famed telling of the retreat that broke an empire.
illustration-of-the-method-of-recording-:
James Owen Dorsey and fellow workers showed how Indian languages were recorded, in this Smithsonian Bureau of Ethnology piece. It draws on manuscripts by Dorsey, A. S. Gatschet, and S. R. Riggs. A key explains the special signs used for sounds not found in English.

An Omaha myth, How the Rabbit Caught the Sun in a Trap, is set out word by word. Each native word sits over its English gloss in lines. Later Dakota lines use the same close method. The piece lets readers see the exact method scholars used to fix speech on paper.
letters-of-marcus-tullius-cicero: This volume gathers the letters of Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman and orator. The Project Gutenberg header gives the title as Letters of Cicero and names Cicero as author. The hosted sample preserves only that header, with no letter texts or contents pages. This note therefore rests on the title and author alone, and makes no claim about which letters the volume holds.
letters-to-helen-impressions-of-an-artis:
Keith Henderson wrote Letters to Helen from the Western Front. Chatto and Windus published them in London in 1917, with his own illustrations. A ruined crucifix corner fronts the book.

His pictures show Bailleul, Fricourt cemetery, and trenches near La Boisselle. A wounded tank and a bursting ammunition dump appear later. The first letter is dated June 6, 1916, aboard a slow train. Henderson writes as an artist watching war change a landscape. Helen receives scenes that mix beauty, mud, and loss. Peronne and the Butte de Warlencourt appear among his subjects. Henderson's drawings record ruins that words alone might miss.
my-friend-prospero:
Henry Harland set this novel in Italy, in a castle above a bright valley. Harland had won fame with The Cardinal's Snuff-Box. John Lane issued the book in 1903, and it sold past a hundred thousand. Lady Blanchemain arrives by coach in sweet April weather.

She studies the formal garden, with terraces, ilex walks, and statues. Below laughs a wild valley of fruit trees and a winding river. Olive hills rise blue-grey on each side. Harland writes with light, lush care for place. Prospero, the friend of the title, waits within this charmed scene, and romance grows in the Italian sun.
nasa-tm-19650009335-compilation-of-calib:
L C Castagnola at Goddard Space Flight Center compiled calibration data for one Aerobee sounding rocket flight. The flight was numbered 4.13 GP-GT and used an Aerobee 150A rocket. It flew as a performance vehicle, heavily fitted with instruments by Goddard staff.

Castagnola gathers the calibration record for that flight in one place. Calibration data link what instruments read to what really happened. Without it, flight readings cannot be trusted or compared. Compilations like this one are working records, kept so the flight data from that mission remain usable afterward.
nasa-tm-19660009052-nasa-s-spacecraft-ba:
Eugene R Stroup and Armin O Apelt describe NASA's program for testing spacecraft batteries, run as applied research with technical management at Goddard. New battery designs are bought, tested, and reported on by the program. About one thousand secondary, or rechargeable, spacecraft cells were in the program at the time. Key parts include acceptance testing, performance checks, and long life-cycling runs.

Failed cells are taken apart and analyzed in detail. What is learned goes back to the maker, to guide design improvements. Results are reported monthly and yearly to users. A spacecraft lives or dies by its batteries in shadow, so this steady test work underwrote many missions.
nasa-tm-19660015353-rocket-measurements-:
David S Evans reported rocket measurements in January 1966 of energetic electrons raining into the auroral zone. Precipitation is the fall of charged particles from space into the upper air. There they strike gases and light the aurora. A rocket can pass through the falling stream and count the electrons directly, at heights no satellite orbit of the era could hold for long.

Ground cameras see the glow, but not the particles causing it. Rocket data link the two views together. Evans presents measurements from the zone where displays are brightest. Such flights built the base of facts about how energy from the magnetosphere reaches the air above the poles.
nasa-tm-19660020786-optimization-of-adia:
J Reece Roth at Lewis Research Center set out design rules for magnetic mirror machines used in fusion research. A mirror machine holds hot plasma between two stronger magnetic fields, like caps on a bottle. His problem is a sharp one: confine the largest number of particles for a given cost. A plasma of stated density and temperature is released at the middle of the machine.

Coil size, field strength, and mirror ratio are then adjusted for the best hold. The plasma is assumed to spread evenly in all directions. Adiabatic confinement means the particles stay trapped without heating tricks. Roth formulates guidelines, not one fixed design, so builders of fusion rigs could size their own machines with care.
nasa-tm-19660024052-experimental-perform:
H W Douglass, G Hennings, and H G Price Jr fired a rocket engine on the fierce pairing of liquid hydrogen and liquid fluorine, for this Langley memorandum. The engine was regeneratively cooled, meaning cold fuel flowed through its walls before burning. Thrust was five thousand pounds, and chamber pressure reached a stated three hundred pounds per square inch. The summary reports performance efficiency of ninety-eight percent.

Their best specific impulse is given in the sample, at a mixture with under fourteen percent hydrogen. That value reached ninety-eight percent of the theoretical maximum. Fluorine promised the highest performance of any chemical oxidizer. Its violence and poison kept it from flight use, but the measured record of what it could do remains striking.
nasa-tm-19700025079-a-design-parameter-s:
NASA issued this general working paper, number 10,084, on the design of a hypothetical lunar flying vehicle. The design values are drawn from a mathematical analysis of the craft. A lunar flyer was a proposed small vehicle for moving astronauts across the Moon's surface, hopping above ground it could not cross.

The analysis starts with the system parameters and the equations behind them, including a describing function for the human pilot. Graphs developed there feed a study of possible vehicle configurations. Results are shown as stability maps and Nyquist plots, two standard ways of picturing control behavior. One section traces how the stable area shifts as the pilot describing parameters change.
nasa-tm-19710000918-scattering-of-42-mev:
William M. Stewart of the Lewis Research Center and K. K. Seth of Northwestern University ran this nuclear study. It fires alpha particles at scandium-45 nuclei and records how they scatter. The work was prepared for a meeting of nuclear physicists.

Scandium-45 had been a puzzle for the shell model of the nucleus. That model placed its lowest excited state higher than tests had found states. A rival rotational model fit the known levels better, the authors note. Their scattering test was run to gain more facts about the nucleus. How its parts move together, called collective behavior, was the trait in question.
nasa-tm-19710007274-topics-in-solar-cosm:
Thomas L. Cline of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in December 1970. It covers topics in how the Sun produces cosmic rays and X rays. Solar flares can flood the space near Earth with fast particles and hard radiation, and sorting out how remains a live question.

Cline builds on observations of solar protons, electrons, and X rays from Goddard satellite experiments. The IMP, OGO, and OSO satellite series supplied the readings, some his own and some passed on from others. Newer instruments saw lower energies, flew beyond the magnetosphere, and watched through much of the solar cycle. The data suggest such particles are made more often than in big flares alone, and in more than one way.
nasa-tm-19710018370-a-concept-for-a-lear:
Juergen K Baumeister of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this concept paper on April 20, 1970, as NASA TM X-64518. He held a National Research Council postdoctoral post in the Astrionics Laboratory. The paper sketches a learning attitude control system for launch vehicles. Such a system would adjust its own steering as flight conditions change.

Baumeister called the concept rough and early. He built it from published studies and his own computer investigations. The design is digital and adaptive, meant for any high performance launcher. He also named the space shuttle and aircraft as possible users. Learning control promised steadier flight when winds or vehicle behavior surprised the crew.
no-hero:
E. W. Hornung published No Hero in 1903, a tale told in thirteen chapters. The first is called A Plenipotentiary, the second The Theatre of War. First Blood, A Little Knowledge, and A Marked Woman follow. Out of Action and Second Fiddle hint at a hero kept from glory.

The narrator opens by musing on the unopened envelope. No writer, he thinks, has dealt with its dramatic side. A friend's face betrays his news at a glance, good or bad. Handwriting on the breakfast table gives no such hint. That sly start sets a tale of war where the hero, by his title, claims no hero's part.
notes-on-a-journey-from-cornhill-to-gran:
William Makepeace Thackeray called his travel book Notes on a Journey from Cornhill to Grand Cairo. He dedicated it to Captain Samuel Lewis of the Peninsular and Oriental service. Grateful passengers give teapots and tankards, he jokes, but authors have paper, not bullion. This small volume is his token for a pleasant voyage.

Chapters call at Vigo, Lisbon, Cadiz, and Gibraltar in turn. Athens follows, then Smyrna, billed as first glimpses of the East. Constantinople, Rhodes, a white squall, and Beyrout come next. A day and night in Syria leads to Jaffa and Jerusalem. Alexandria and Cairo close the road. Thackeray narrates with ease and irony.
peter-a-novel-of-which-he-is-not-the-her:
F. Hopkinson Smith called his book Peter: A Novel of Which He is Not the Hero. Peter is an elderly clerk at the Exeter bank, poring over his ledger one December afternoon. The narrator, his friend of eleven years, finds him still at work past the hour of their daily walk uptown, his bald head glistening like an ostrich egg under the gas jets.

The bank itself is a mouldy, out-of-date barn, unpainted for half a century. Around gentle Peter and the young people he quietly helps, Smith builds a story of old New York banking and unselfish goodness. Peter steers others' happiness while claiming none of the credit.
podcast-joerogan-OMzjWh96wro:
Doctor Peter Attia joins Joe Rogan and tells how he nearly worked for Theranos in a segment from the show. Attia is a doctor focused on long life and health span. Theranos was the blood-test firm that fell in fraud and shame.

Attia tells how close he came to a job with the firm and what saved him from the wreck. He shares what the near miss taught him about hype in health tech. Rogan draws out the red flags Attia saw, or missed, at the time. Listeners get a sharp tale of a bullet dodged. The library holds the segment as an archive record.
podcast-joerogan-rx72my2DMro:
Episode 6 of Joe Rogan Questions Everything, presented in audio-only form, pairs Rogan with Duncan Trussell once more. The TV spin-off sent Rogan chasing strange claims with a comic sidekick. Trussell's job was to keep the hunt funny while Rogan asked the questions.

The two chase the weird together, from Bigfoot lore to ghosts and other fringe claims. Trussell jokes through the evidence while still showing real curiosity. Rogan tries to sort honest witnesses from true believers and fakes. The episode shows the playful side of Rogan's mystery habit, long before the podcast ruled his career.
prehistoric-textile-fabrics-of-the-unite:
William H. Holmes wrote this Smithsonian study for the Bureau of Ethnology, reconstructing prehistoric American weaving from a ghost archive. The impressions that fabrics left in wet clay before the pots were fired. The cloth itself rotted away centuries ago, yet its weave survives pressed into pottery across the United States. Holmes sorts the finds into six groups plus miscellaneous finds, with plates showing pottery fragments and the textile patterns stamped upon them.

Each group records a technique: plain weaving, twining, and more complex structures, from peoples who left no written word about their looms. The report treats a pot shard as a page of industrial history, from which fiber, thread, and method can be read. Archaeologists still cite Holmes on American textiles; his insight, that the humblest craft evidence can outlast monuments, begins in studies exactly like this one.
roman-farm-management-the-treatises-of-c:
Cato's and Varro's treatises on farming are done into English here by a Virginia farmer, with notes of modern instances, in a book dated 1918. Two opening notes treat the Roman agronomists and Virgil's debt to Varro. Cato's De Agricultura then fills the first part, in a full synopsis.

Cato's heads run from the dignity of the farmer to buying a farm and laying it out. Duties of the owner, the overseer, the housekeeper, and the hands follow. Draining, seed beds, manure, soil improvement, forage crops, pastures, and the care of live stock fill the working list. Varro's three books, Rerum Rusticarum Libri Tres, form the second part.
roman-life-in-the-days-of-cicero:
The Reverend Alfred J. Church, author of Stories from Homer, tells of Roman life in the days of Cicero for young readers, with illustrations. He dedicates the book to Octavius Ogle, in remembrance of a long friendship. Fifteen chapters move from private life to the great figures of the age.

A Roman Boy and A Roman Undergraduate open the set, then In the Days of the Dictator and A Roman Magistrate. A Great Roman Cause and A Great Conspiracy frame the public drama. Caesar, Pompey, Cato, Brutus and Porcia, and Atticus each take a chapter. Exile, a governor in his province, and Antony and Augustus close the survey of Cicero's world.
social-life-at-rome-in-the-age-of-cicero:
W. Warde Fowler wrote Social Life at Rome in the Age of Cicero. He aimed to fill a gap in English books on Rome. Schools teach the great writers of the Republic's last age. They also teach its rule and laws. No English book, though, drew its life and ways. Fowler covers schooling, morals, and faith in that age.

His chief source is Cicero's own correspondence. More than nine hundred letters from the time survive. He also leans on Marquardt's work on Roman private life. The labors of Tyrrell and Purser helped him as well. The book was first meant as a mate to Tucker's Life in Ancient Athens. That plan was dropped before the work was done.
successful-exploration-through-the-inter:
Successful Exploration Through the Interior of Australia came out at London in 1863. Richard Bentley printed it. It tells the Burke and Wills expedition from Melbourne to the Gulf of Carpentaria. It tells it through the journals and letters of William John Wills. His father, William Wills, edited the book and dedicated it to the Duke of Newcastle.

The preface explains that the younger Wills was second in command of the famous expedition, serving as astronomer, topographer, journalist, and surveyor across eighteen hundred miles of country no European had trodden. His father praises the skill with which he guided the march, and his courage, patience, and heroic death in the desert, where he asked to be left alone.
the-aeroplane-boys-on-the-wing-or-aeropl: John Luther Langworthy wrote The Aeroplane Boys on the Wing in 1912. Its subtitle is Aeroplane Chums in the Tropics. A front note plugs the third book of the set. That book is The Bird Boys Among the Clouds. Chapters listed start with On the Way Back from the Game. Frank's Way and A Startling Discovery follow. The Devil-Bird stands midway. The Airship Launched at Last closes the list.
the-amours-of-zeokinizul-king-of-the-kof:
The Amours of Zeokinizul, King of the Kofirans was printed in London for G. Smith near Temple-Bar in 1749. It was priced at one shilling and sixpence. The book claims to be turned into English from the Arabic of a famed traveller named Krinelbol. A key is supplied with the text. Its preface is credited to the bookseller who pushed the work into print.

That preface jokes that a preface is as needful to a book as an opening to a sermon, though few read the one or heed the other. It insists the little work sets truth in a just light, while warning readers against false readings laid on its figures. Such caution fits a veiled court satire dressed in foreign names.
the-composition-of-indian-geographical-n:
J. Hammond Trumbull studies how Indian geographical names are built, drawing his examples from the Algonkin languages. The Hartford press of Case, Lockwood and Brainard printed the work, and a transcriber's note dates it 1870. Special marks in the original, the note explains, are rendered with signs such as an equals mark for a long vowel.

Trumbull opens by testing a common definition. A proper name, some hold, is a mere mark put on an individual, and its chief property is to be destitute of meaning. If that definition held, he argues, there would be no proper names in the aboriginal languages at all. The essay that follows shows the opposite: place names in those languages carry packed, descriptive sense. His evidence comes word by word, breaking names into their parts.
the-education-of-the-negro:
Charles Dudley Warner's essay The Education of the Negro takes up the state of Black citizens after the Civil War. At the war's close, he writes, about five million Black folk gained citizenship; by the census of 1890 they numbered over seven and a half million. The ballot came at once, with no test of schooling or property.

Warner weighs why the South first fought that change, then evaded it. He asks what schooling can fit a freed people for full civic life. His views mark his age, and the essay shows how white reformers framed the question.
the-great-events-by-famous-historians-vo: The Great Events by Famous Historians retells world history in the words of eminent historians. This record is Volume VI of the set. It was issued as a limited edition by the National Alumni. Only front matter is present here: a binding note and the title page. The binding copies an original in the Bibliotheque Nationale, Paris. Geoffroy Tory made it for King Francis I. His device, a broken vase, stands for the frailty of the body. A picture shows the death of Archbishop Becket. No contents list is present.
the-history-of-england-in-three-volumes-: The History of England, Volume II, bears the name of David Hume on its title page. James S. Virtue printed it in London in 1860. A second title page makes the division clear. Volume II continues the history by Tobias Smollett, M.D. It runs from William and Mary to the death of George II. Frontispiece and map lists also appear. They name Marlborough and maps of India and Scotland. Only the title pages and illustration lists are present here.
the-knights-of-the-white-shield-up-the-l: Edward A. Rand wrote this boys' club story for the Up-the-Ladder Club series, dated 1886 and dedicated to Ken and the other boys. Only the title pages and contents are present here. The story itself does not appear. The contents follow a Sunday school club through its year. Making a club opens them. An offer for scholars and the nation's birthday follow. A sick patriot comes next. The entertainment, the cupola, and Aunt Stanshy's boarder appear. The club in splinters and the club mended close the list.
the-ladies-work-book-containing-instruct: John Cassell published this ladies' work-book in London, from La Belle Sauvage Yard on Ludgate Hill. The book teaches knitting, crochet, and point-lace. Only the title page and list of illustrations are present here. The instructions themselves do not appear. The list reads as a first lesson plan. Casting on with one needle and with two comes first. Plain knitting, the German manner, and purling follow. Making a stitch and taking up stitches come next. Projects include an infant's shoe and anti-macassars.
the-last-journals-of-david-livingstone-i:
Horace Waller edited David Livingstone last journals, issued in London in 1874 after the explorer death in Central Africa. Volume one covers 1866 to 1868, with portrait, maps, and illustrations. Waller introduction says the journals survived thanks to faithful attendants who carried them out.

A closing narrative from servants Chuma and Susi covers Livingstone last moments and sufferings. The journals record the search for where the Nile truly rises, across seven years of travel. Readers get daily notes, geography, and a first hand record of hardship in country then little mapped by Europeans.
the-life-studies-and-works-of-benjamin-w:
John Galt composed the life, studies, and works of Benjamin West from materials West furnished himself, in a book dated 1820. His preface, dated April 25, 1816, explains a change of plan. West later career belongs so fully to the public history of art that Galt detached the early memoirs as a whole by themselves.

West rose without a teacher, and Galt argues that his self taught path helps young artists more than fine lectures could. West served as president of the Royal Academy in London. Part one follows an American painter from colonial beginnings toward history painting fame.
the-little-colonel-s-hero: The Little Colonel's Hero by Annie Fellows Johnston carries a 1902 copyright from the Page Company of Boston, with a frontispiece by Etheldred B. Barry. Only the title pages, impression lists, and dedication are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The dedication addresses all the friends of the Little Colonel whose letters the author could not answer. Printed impression lists run from the twenty-seventh in 1925 to the thirty-fifth in 1937, showing how long the book stayed in print.
the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-volume-0:
Volume six of Suetonius's Lives of the Twelve Caesars covers Nero Claudius Caesar, in Alexander Thomson's translation revised by T. Forester. Suetonius opens with the Domitii, the family behind Nero. One branch, the Aenobarbi, took both descent and name from Lucius Domitius, whose black hair was stroked by two godlike young men announcing a victory, and turned the bright color of brass.

That mark, Suetonius says, descended to his posterity, who generally had red beards. The family collected seven consulships, one triumph, and two censorships. They also used only two first names, Cneius and Lucius, swapping them in an irregular pattern across generations. Family pride and oddity come first, before Nero's own story begins.
the-negro:
W. E. B. Du Bois's The Negro was published in New York by Holt in 1915. Only front matter and the bare opening of its first chapter are present here. The survey itself does not appear. A transcriber's note warns that hyphenation and accents are inconsistent in the electronic text and may not match the 1915 edition exactly, advising researchers to verify spellings elsewhere. A dedication to a faithful helper, initialled M. G. A., follows the title.

Contents shown name only suggestions for further reading, plus four maps: the physical geography of Africa, its ancient kingdoms, its races, and the distribution of Negro blood, ancient and modern. Chapter I, Africa, begins with the single word Behold! before the pages end.
the-original-fables-of-la-fontaine-rende: Fredk. Colin Tilney rendered the original fables of La Fontaine into English prose, with coloured illustrations by the author himself. The book belongs to a series called Tales for Children from Many Lands, edited by F. C. Tilney, from Dent in London and Dutton in New York. Only the front matter and the start of the contents are present here, so the fables themselves do not appear. The contents open with The Two Mules and The Hare and the Partridge.
the-water-supply-of-the-el-paso-and-sout:
J. L. Campbell presented his paper on the El Paso and Southwestern Railway's water supply to the American Society of Civil Engineers in May 1910. The described system serves the division between Carrizozo and Santa Rosa in New Mexico, a distance of 128 miles across arid country west of the hundredth meridian. Discussion by G. E. P. Smith and Kenneth Allan accompanies the paper.

Average annual precipitation is given as 9.84 inches, and exceptionally dry 1909 saw less than five. Wells from 100 to 1,100 feet deep originally supplied the road, but their water stayed bad after thorough treatment. Campbell lists the damage plainly: violent foaming, hard scaling, destroyed boiler tubes, engine failures, and demoralised train service.
young-folks-treasury-volume-2-of-12-myth: Hamilton Wright Mabie edited this twelve-volume Young Folks' Treasury, with Edward Everett Hale as associate editor. Volume two covers myths and legendary heroes. Pages present here hold title pages and a list of editors, contributors, and advisers, but no tales. The advisers list names Theodore Roosevelt, Grover Cleveland, and Cardinal Gibbons. A pictured caption shows Jason hurling his helmet. The myths and hero tales themselves do not appear in these pages.
